The effectiveness of these approaches was validated through simulations and real-world applications, revealing that alternative splicing can be regulated by distinct mechanisms, including the exclusion or inclusion of exons, the use of different transcriptional start sites, and the production of different mRNA isoforms. The findings suggest that alternative splicing is a versatile mechanism for regulating gene expression in response to various environmental and developmental stimuli.

In Europe, specific laws and regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation and the Law on Processing of Personal Data and Protection of Personal Data Information in Bulgaria, govern data privacy standards. A recent survey conducted in 2020 highlighted a significant gap in understanding the non-technical aspects of these laws among IT professionals. Focusing on the technical aspects of data privacy compliance, this research investigates the perspectives of various stakeholders on implementing measures to ensure GDPR compliance. Based on qualitative interviews with 10 IT professionals, the study reveals a lack of understanding among them regarding non-technical aspects of data protection laws. According to the findings, technical professionals primarily rely on non-specialized sources to comprehend the laws, whereas technical compliance requires an understanding of the legal standards, which poses a challenge due to the existing resources available.

The observation of particle correlations in $pA$ collisions, specifically in the range of a few GeV, suggests that interactions between the projectile proton, target nucleus, and produced particles are crucial for understanding these processes. Our research examines the relationship between the projectile proton, target nucleus, and produced particles based on their azimuthal angles, taking into account the effects of particle momentum and mass. We have developed a method to measure the frequency of angular pair relationships between the proton, nucleus, and pairs of particles, using a new method that accounts for background noise. We have applied this method to data from the ALICE collaboration and found that the frequency of angular pair relationships is consistent with a scenario in which the phase space of the collision is evenly distributed. We have also compared our findings with theoretical models that describe the effects of a magnetic field produced by the target nucleus on the charged particles.

The production of light nuclei in high-energy collisions can be explained through various coalescence models, which all agree that baryon conservation is crucial. In this study, we examined the coalescence models' predictions for Au-Au collisions at 3 GeV, using the MCGLE calculations to understand hadron production. We found that coalescence models can accurately describe hadron spectra, elliptic flow, and coalescence parameters, but not elliptic flow differences between odd and even particles. Notably, coalescence models can also accurately describe light nuclei and their ratios, suggesting that baryon conservation is a key factor in their production. However, this model has limitations in explaining certain features of light nuclei and their ratios, indicating that additional processes, such as hadron interactions, are necessary to fully understand their creation.

The discovery of thousands of exoplanets has made it clear that our solar system's unique planetary arrangement is a rare occurrence in the universe. Researchers believe that the presence of a habitable planet within a specific zoned planetary system, where a star is powered by its core, will be the key factor in determining the presence of life on such planets. Our research suggests that the atmospheres of these habitable planets will be shaped by their proximity to the star, resulting in an uneven distribution of heat. However, if a planet is located at a distance where its atmosphere is in thermal balance with the surrounding environment, it will experience a dynamic and constantly changing atmosphere, with strong vertical and horizontal temperature gradients. On the other hand, if a planet is located closer to the star, its atmosphere will be extremely hot and dense, and if farther away, it will be extremely cold and dense. In either case, life as we know it would likely struggle to thrive.

The dispersal function of a set of vertices measures the variety of distances those vertices have to every other vertex. A graph is highly dispersible if there is a set of vertices that has a unique distance to every other vertex. We identify the smallest set of vertices that makes a circulant graph dispersible for any size. A particular type of circulant graph called a primitive root circulant requires a special property and is more likely to be dispersible. We provide a simpler method to check if a given set of vertices in this type of graph makes the graph dispersible and show that a set of two vertices is sufficient for dispersability for the specific circulant graph of order 12 with a special set of roots.

The efficient computation of the inverse of sparse matrices is crucial in numerous applications, particularly in the context of finite element methods where non-singular, real and symmetric matrices are often employed. To address this need, an iterative matrix inversion method has been developed, utilizing an enhanced version of Dassss and an optimized Dass3 algorithm. These updated methods incorporate a novel approach to eliminating Gaussian elimination steps, resulting in a significant reduction in computation time. Furthermore, the algorithms have been optimized for high-performance processing on graphics processing units, leveraging the use of half-precision arithmetic and minimizing synchronization barriers. Performance comparisons with the popular Mattel6 method reveal that these novel methods not only accelerate computation by 1.7 times, but also reduce memory requirements by 1.3 times.

This paper delves into the power spectrum of tensor and scalar fluctuations produced by tensor and scalar fluctuations, a novel inflationary scenario exhibiting a dual ultra-slow-roll and a slow-roll regime, where a transition from an ultra-slow-roll regime to a slow-roll regime occurs. A perturbative approach is employed to analyze the power spectrum, considering the impact of non-perturbative effects in the slow-roll regime. Notably, the power spectrum is found to be continuous at the transition point between the two regimes. It has been demonstrated that, in the context of this inflationary scenario, the power spectrum of tensor fluctuations is lower than the power spectrum of scalar fluctuations. Furthermore, the power spectrum of tensor fluctuations is found to be lower than the power spectrum of scalar fluctuations in the slow-roll regime. A numerical comparison has been performed with the slow-roll approximation, revealing that, in the ultra-slow-roll regime, the power spectrum of tensor fluctuations is lower than the power spectrum of scalar fluctuations is lower than the power spectrum of tensor fluctuations in the slow-roll regime.

The primary goal of the Assortment Optimization problem is to select a subset of products to offer, with the aim of maximizing revenue from sales. This paper introduces a more complex version of this problem, known as the Enhanced Assortment Optimization problem, where the impact of adding or removing a product is taken into account. This expanded problem is more representative of real-world scenarios where products can be rebranded or updated. By focusing on a more general case involving concave utility, this paper develops an approximate solution using a convex optimization technique, resulting in an algorithm that stops and provides a precise estimate of the optimal outcome. In a more specific case involving a submodular revenue model, this paper shows that a more efficient algorithm is applicable and provides exact results.

The casebase approach is a straightforward yet efficient method for analyzing time-to-event data that can be applied across various settings. This non-parametric method is particularly useful for predicting survival rates and determining the effectiveness of treatments, especially when dealing with rare events. It has a substantial body of evidence supporting its reliability, as it is based on the principles of counting. In this study, we introduce a novel method for comparing survival rates using casebase analysis and evaluate its performance by simulating various scenarios with known outcomes. We also conduct casebase analyses on two real-world datasets to examine the incidence of sepsis and the efficacy of vancomycin in treating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia.

High-precision theoretical calculations in particle physics require advanced methods to compute loop integrals with diverse topological structures and complex mass scales. This complexity is addressed by multi-scale Feynman integrals, which can be precisely defined and calculated through scale-anomaly calculations. In this study, a comprehensive and efficient approach to evaluate such integrals is presented, complemented by Mathematica and FeyArborizer codes. This method is applied to several two- and three-loop examples, demonstrating its capabilities and reliability. Notably, it enables the exact computation of three-loop massless Feynman integrals, with implications for future high-precision projects that will certainly benefit from similar calculations.

The performance of Object Storage Systems (OSS) has garnered significant interest from scientific community. The main advantage of OSS is its ability to handle objects with diverse characteristics, making it a suitable option for managing large, unstructured data. Although OSS has its benefits, it is still not widely used in scientific applications due to performance issues. In this study, we evaluate the performance of two OSS approaches, namely, a hierarchical object store and a non-hierarchical object store, using DAOS and Lustre. The results indicate that the non-hierarchical object store outperforms the hierarchical store, especially under heavy loads. Additionally, both approaches provide better performance than Lustre for small objects and high throughput scenarios. However, Lustre excelled in handling large objects and multiple threads. The findings of this study can be applied to the development of efficient object data management systems for scientific applications.

The widespread adoption of electric vehicles is transforming our daily lives. As their use continues to evolve, the need for efficient public charging infrastructure is becoming more apparent. To address this need, this research proposes an access control system that enables standardization and interoperability across different EV charging station systems. The proposed system utilizes cloud-based credentials, ensuring a scalable solution, and incorporates a single central server for seamless integration. The system's architecture is highly adaptable and can be tailored to various operational models. The core components of the system include a cloud-based identifier, a cloud-based permission manager, and an EV, all of which are illustrated through a practical use case. The proposed system's benefits and implications are also discussed.

This research focuses on developing linear code structures that exhibit maximal correlation distance properties. The study shows that certain types of these codes do not exist in prime fields but can be generated using a construction method. A specific subset of these codes, denoted as the $[n, k, d]$ LCD code, has been identified. The research provides conditions for creating such code structures and presents examples of their implementation. Additionally, several numerical examples have been presented to demonstrate the practical application of these code systems.

The Equivalence Theorem, valid in General Relativity with certain constraints, allows us to compare Loop Quantum Gravity with the standard Einstein theory in specific low-energy limit. In this study, we demonstrate that the EFT of Loop Quantum Gravity, when the scalar mode is suppressed, effectively reduces to the standard Einstein theory. By examining the EFT, we can derive the Equivalence Theorem, providing new insights into the LQG EFT. Additionally, we investigate the EFT in various scenarios, such as decoupling the scalar mode or introducing a mass gap, and find that the leading order term remains the traditional Einstein theory.

A study focusing on the American West assesses the impact of shifting power generation away from urban areas towards desert locations. The research considers the integration of renewable energy with nuclear power and evaluates various factors influencing the decision to invest in nuclear facilities. It has been observed that desert locations with high solar radiation are less competitive due to the underutilization of land for solar power. The study's model, which accounts for land competition, directs new nuclear investments towards desert areas previously neglected. The study's findings, which prioritize land efficiency in choosing new nuclear sites, align with the existing preference for selecting locations based on other factors like climate and infrastructure. The research highlights the need for a comprehensive approach that takes into account both energy efficiency and land efficiency in decision-making.

Cluster-randomized trials are frequently employed to assess the efficacy of vaccines 
and antiviral medications. Estimating the proportion of individuals who will not develop a specific disease under treatment, as well as the associated prediction interval, is a primary goal of these trials. However, analyzing cluster-randomized trials poses a unique challenge due to their inherent structure. A recent publication in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute's Statistical Science section has explored the application of frequentist methods for this purpose. The authors propose a method for estimating mean compliance and develop a new approach for adjusting for the inherent structure of these trials. They also provide asymptotic expressions for the associated confidence intervals. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the performance of these methods and found that they produced accurate results. Furthermore, the methods were applied to a real-world example, a large-scale cluster-randomized trial of the bivalent HPV vaccine, resulting in the derivation of estimated mean compliance and confidence intervals for the treated population.

Research on fractal networks has gained significant attention, driven by the discovery of their unique characteristics. This interest stems from the fact that fractal networks can offer the same services as traditional networks at lower costs. Notably, the study of fractal networks has expanded to include their application in the field of energy. This paper focuses on analyzing the normalized Laplacian spectrum of the Mobius octagonal network, a specific fractal network, within the $n$-stage range. By establishing a relationship between this network and its inner fractal sub-network, a linear recurrence relation is derived, enabling the calculation of the normalized Laplacian polynomial. Furthermore, the normalized Laplacian function is obtained, and its implications on the energy band gap of the network are explored. This research also provides a comparison with the regular octagonal network, highlighting its advantages.

Contextual linear bandits is a key model in online learning with vast practical applications, often involving large-scale deployments where multiple servers operate independently within separate regions. In this setup, a critical question arises: how can online learning algorithms effectively function in distributed contexts without requiring the full knowledge of the underlying problem setting. To tackle this issue, we explore how the sample complexities of online learning algorithms for contextual linear bandits behave under a decentralized framework. Specifically, we consider a scenario where multiple servers, each operating within a local region, can exchange limited information. To this end, we introduce a \emph{shared covariance matrix} assumption and a \emph{shared reward} assumption that reflect real-world scenarios, where servers can exchange information on covariances but not rewards. Under both settings, we provide sample complexity lower bounds and an optimal distributed algorithm, thus establishing the first sample complexity results for linear contextual bandits in a distributed framework.

Healthcare and medical research heavily rely on Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which provide essential data for tasks like identifying patient cohorts and predicting health outcomes. However, the scarcity and restricted availability of EHRs hinder the efficient use of available data, such as data from patient registries, for research and development purposes. To address this issue, we investigate the synthesis of realistic and comprehensive EHRs for Cystic Fibrosis patients, utilizing a data-driven approach. This study involves three phases: (1) constructing a Cystic Fibrosis patient registry, (2) developing a data synthesis framework, and (3) evaluating synthetic EHRs through comparison with real-world clinical data. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, and we anticipate its broader applicability to diverse clinical data sets.

The $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\mp \pi^\mp$ decay process is examined using $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb detector, which corresponds to a total integrated luminosity of 6 fb$^{-1}$, and is operated at centre-of-mass energies of 7, 8 and 13 TeV. The $D^0$ mesons in this study are produced in the decay $D^0 \to K^+ K^- \pi^-\$, and are subject to various selection criteria and two different sets of isobarial fits, which enable the measurement of the $D^0$ branching fraction into $K^\mp\pi^\pm\pi^\mp$ as $(7.7\pm 0.8\pm 0.5 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-3}$.

The purpose of this study is to introduce Novelpy, a Python package that calculates and assesses the novelty and and disruptiveness of bibliometric and patent data. By employing a comparative text analysis of abstracts from existing and emerging research against that of preceding and subsequent studies, Novelpy quantifies the magnitude of changes in text similarity. This approach yields a continuous measure of novelty and disruptiveness that can be correlated with established bibliometric indicators, such as citation counts and impact factor. The paper outlines Novelpy's technical framework and showcases its functionality through a live demonstration and accompanying dataset, making it easier for researchers to replicate and build upon the findings. The author encourages collaboration and expansion of the package's capabilities to facilitate research in the fields of science studies, history of science, and innovation policy, as well as other relevant domains.

Achieving complete control over the intensity of light is a fundamental aspect of optics that has been extensively explored in various research applications, such as manipulating chemical reactions and quantum information processing. However, controlling the intensity of multiple spatial modes of light simultaneously poses a significant challenge. We have developed a versatile method that enables the precise control of multiple laser beams by utilizing the nonlinear interactions between the beams. This approach offers several benefits, including the ability to manipulate an arbitrary number of beams with minimal resources, versatility in beam configurations, and the capacity to be integrated with existing systems. The method's efficacy has been confirmed through successful experimental implementation, demonstrating its potential in managing a multitude of laser beams.

This study investigates the suitability of conventional methods for integrating existing components in robotic archery, and highlights the challenges and potential solutions in robot design, with a focus on recurve archery. The difficulties in designing robots for this precise task arise due to the delicate balance and variability in human performance, a characteristic that is often achieved by adjusting techniques to suit individual skills. Presently, robots operate under ideal and uniform conditions, a far cry from the reality of a competitive archery setting. Consequently, the research undertakes to identify the sources of the gap between human and robotic performance, to inform the development of a prototype robot that can shoot a recurve bow.

The main goal of cross-domain recommendation systems is to enhance the accuracy of target domain predictions by utilizing knowledge from the source domain. A common approach involves first extracting source domain information and then using it to inform target domain model training through joint learning. However, this approach often results in target domain overfitting due to the strong influence of the source domain. To address this limitation, we suggest a novel method called dual metric training, which enables the target model to focus on the target loss while allowing the source loss to influence it selectively. To achieve this, we propose a metric learning technique that allows the target loss to control the target model's parameters, while the source loss can adjust the weights of the source and target embeddings in a way that minimizes their discrepancy. Through experimentation on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation systems, offering both improved performance and increased efficiency.

The logical language used to describe asynchronous distributed machines, a subset of the propositional modal mu-calculus, has the potential to capture the behavior of systems that operate independently and interactively. A specific component of this language, the modal mu-free fragment, has been proven to have a clear definition based on the evaluation of a specific type of function in a specific order. This study investigates a broader subset of the language, which is used to describe asynchronous distributed machines, and it presents evidence that its functions have distinct characteristics. This discovery provides a specific and useful way to determine whether a given language expression corresponds to the concept of an asynchronous distributed machine. This finding has significant implications for the development of tools that analyze the logic, which can now be designed using more efficient and streamlined methods.

Our research examines the transfer of heat at a steady-state condition within two-dimensional layers of a complex plasma. The simulations were conducted using the thermal lattice-boltzmann method, which was applied in a geometrically non-uniform setup. The results show that the thermal diffusion coefficient varies in proportion to temperature gradients within the layer, but its overall behavior is characterized by a thermally-driven drift motion that opposes temperature gradients. The simulations also reveal that the layer acts as a heat reservoir, maintaining a relatively constant temperature. When heated, the layer becomes denser at its core and less dense at its edges, due to a phenomenon known as thermal diffusion cooling.

We investigate whether combining separate pieces of information, each considered valuable on its own, through a linear process can sometimes result in unexpected loss of insight. Focusing on the most straightforward form of combination - linear computation - we develop methods to accurately restore the original input components from a computed outcome. Our approach has broad applications, including data analysis, machine learning algorithms, and statistical models. Crucially, it also sheds light on the inherent connections between specific mathematical concepts and offers a practical solution for reconstructing information in various types of computational analyses.

Cardiac angiography via fluoroscopy is a common procedure used to diagnose and treat heart conditions, but it comes with the drawback of high X-ray radiation exposure, which can be detrimental to both patients and medical staff. Although this issue is well-documented, the exact extent of radiation exposure during the procedure is still not fully understood. By developing a deep-learning based approach to video interpolation, researchers have found a way to reduce the radiation exposure rate without compromising image quality. This innovative method uses a recurrent neural network to generate missing frames in a video, effectively doubling the time between X-ray exposures without additional hardware requirements. The technique was tested on 1000 clinical cardiac angiography videos and proved effective in reducing the radiation exposure rate. This breakthrough has significant implications for the future of cardio-angiography, enabling a balance between optimal image quality and reduced radiation exposure.

The formation of a weakly-coupled quark-gluon plasma in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions is an area of significant theoretical and experimental interest. Confinement of heavy quarks within the quark-gluon plasma poses a significant challenge to our understanding of the phenomenon and is a key aspect to studying the properties of the plasma itself. In this presentation, we will be discussing recent research focused on heavy quark production in high-energy collisions and what insights can be gained through studying the properties of the plasma in high-energy collisions. I will also touch on the opportunities and challenges associated with the heavy-flavor program at the proposed FCC-ee collider, as well as the contribution of heavy quark physics to understanding the properties of the plasma.

We have explored the effects of the tau neutrino mass on the neutrinoless double beta decay in a theoretical framework that combines the dark sector with a leptophilic U(1) particle. The study revealed that the minimal U(1) model, which links the dark sector to the visible sector through U(1)_X = U(1)_{L_e + L_\mu + L_{\tau}} or U(1)_Z = U(1)_{L_e + L_\tau - L_\mu}, can significantly alter the predicted limits on the neutrinoless double beta decay in the standard model. The study also found that the U(1)_Z model can be ruled out by the neutrino mass limits in the dark sector, which is in line with the recent experimental results from the Fermi-LAT experiment.

The formation of binary systems containing a black hole and a massive star can create stellar ejections that could be identified as hypervelocity stars. These ejections could account for a significant portion of the detected hypervelocity stars in the galaxy. A study of the influence of a binary system consisting of a black hole and a star on the motion of nearby stars reveals that the star's orbit is affected, particularly in the case of massive stars, which can experience a change in their orbital radius of up to 100%. The large variation in orbital radius introduces a significant perturbation in the radial velocity of the star, resulting in a difference of up to a factor of 10 between the pre- and post-perturbation velocities. The acceleration of the star due to the perturbation can also be detected, particularly in the case of nearby stars with a large difference in mass, such as a black hole and a star with a mass ratio of 10. The acceleration can be detected, particularly in the case of the most massive star with a mass ratio of 10, which can be used to determine the mass of the central black hole. The presence of a massive star in the vicinity of the black hole can also be detected, particularly in the case of the most massive star with a mass ratio of 10, which can be used to determine the mass of the central black hole. The presence of a massive star in the vicinity of the black hole can also be used to determine the mass of the central

This paper explores a specific class of multiplicative stochastic differential equations related to fractional Brownian motion, focusing on weak solutions. The paper makes a significant contribution by establishing the existence of weak solutions for these SDEs under relatively relaxed conditions that are more specific to the regularization method used rather than the solution itself. The approach taken in the paper is grounded in the theory of regularization by disturbance.

We investigate how specific forcing axioms impact the properties of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$. Our study involves the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) and its variants, including Proper Forcing Axialm (PFAxal), whose known implications for the nonstationary ideal are maximized when $x$ is a closed uncountable set. We demonstrate that in the context of PFAxal, this relationship is indeed optimal. Additionally, we introduce a new forcing axiom, PFAxal+, and show that it yields the same bounds for the properties of the nonstationary ideal as PFAxal. We also explore the consistency of a strong version of PFAxal+, which asserts that every subset of $\omega_1$ that is closed under finite unions and countable intersections is stationary.

Recent breakthroughs in NLP tasks have shown that fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) in task-specific settings can achieve impressive results. However, this approach has its limitations, especially when dealing with novel tasks that have limited or no available data. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed zero-shot generalization frameworks that can leverage PLMs to tackle unseen tasks without prior data. Although these frameworks have shown promise, they often fail to adapt PLMs to tasks with limited or no available data. To address this issue, we introduce the Adaptor framework, a goal-centric approach that enables PLMs to perform novel tasks without requiring task-specific data. The Adaptor framework utilizes a continuous space of tasks, allowing PLMs to adapt to new tasks by interpolating between known tasks. By doing so, it can generalize to unseen tasks with minimal data or no available data at all. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Adaptor framework, we conducted a comprehensive study across various tasks, including text generation, classification, and retrieval. The results demonstrate that Adaptor outperforms existing zero-shot generalization frameworks by a significant margin, with improvements ranging from 8.2% to 28.2%.

The increasing prevalence of shared vehicle services and autonomous vehicles necessitates accurate worldwide traffic signal detection and classification. Current research primarily focuses on datasets collected in North America, leaving a significant knowledge gap in other regions. To address this, a comprehensive traffic signal dataset featuring 1.2 million images from 196 countries has been compiled from the Mapillary platform. This dataset is the first of its kind to incorporate annotated data from over 1,000 distinct locations, enabling more comprehensive studies on traffic signal detection and classification. By leveraging this dataset, which is available for free through the Open Geospatial Consortium, researchers can conduct cross-country comparisons and analyze the global distribution of traffic signals. This can help identify the locations that require the most support for self-driving vehicles.

Recent advancements in representation learning have significantly enhanced the performance of collaborative filtering (CF) recommendations by capturing complex user and item representations within large-scale datasets. However, traditional CF methods face a significant limitation in their ability to generalize across various scenarios due to their reliance on explicit data during the training process. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring novel approaches that utilize implicit data in a self-supervised manner, leveraging only observed user-action-item interactions for representation learning. This study proposes a straightforward self-supervised CF framework, denoted as SelfCF, which focuses on maximizing the mutual information between user and item representations within observed interaction data. Through experiments on multiple real-world datasets, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of SelfCF in outperforming its supervised counterparts in traditional CF approaches.

We have established that the $\mathbb{Q}$-connected components of the generalized Tevelev moduli space associated with degree $d$ del Pezzo surfaces, where $d$ is greater than or equal to $2$, correspond to the open affine models of degree $d$ Del Pezzo surfaces containing a specific type of curve. This result resolves a long-standing problem initially posed by D. Chodosh.

We introduce a novel gapped Dirac semimetal that features linear and quadratic dispersions intermingled. This unique structure of dispersions gives rise to topologically rich properties, including a gapless Weyl point and non-Weyl band inversions. Our comprehensive analysis, grounded in topological invariants and Chern numbers, reveals that the topological transition is driven by the crossing of the linear and quadratic bands, which in turn triggers the inversion of specific bands. Our findings offer a clear pathway for discovering a new class of topological materials.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of slow, semi-stable curves in the hyperbolic plane, focusing on the paths that these curves follow as they enter and exit the influence of the slow curve. Our study reveals that these paths tend towards a pattern where points initially converge towards the center of the curve and then spread out in a radial direction, with velocities that approach the speed of the slow curve. Notably, in the simplest case of a curve with the same speed throughout (a Reeb chord), these entering and exiting trajectories take the form of a logarithmic spiral.

Future ground-based gravitational-wave detectors are expected to be able to detect gravitational waves at higher frequencies, which could reveal new information about the gravitational behavior of space-time. Specifically, certain "gravitational wave harmonics" could provide valuable insights into the behavior of space-time at very high densities, which is a topic of interest due to ongoing research into fundamental physics and cosmology. In this study, we investigate the potential for detecting these wave harmonics using the planned Cosmic Explorer detector, and find that they could be detectable at distances of up to 800 Mpc, which is a significant improvement on previous estimates. Furthermore, the detection of these wave harmonics would provide a significant new window of insight into the behavior of space-time at these high densities.

The second installment of a series "Weighing the Shadows" presents the results of a comprehensive study on Gaia's astrometric detection capabilities for incomplete orbits, relying on simulated data from the Gaia Early Data Release 3. Our investigation involved the analysis of 875 known binaries across 13 diverse systems, encompassing both main sequence and evolved stars, to assess the astrometric monitoring capabilities of Gaia. Our findings suggest that Gaia's astrometry is a reliable tool for identifying partial orbits in a wide range of systems, particularly in high-mass systems, where the orbit's visibility is not impeded by significant brightness disparities. Conversely, in lower mass systems, the flux ratio poses a significant challenge to orbit observation, particularly in systems with orbital periods exceeding 100 years. Nonetheless, our study reveals that even in systems with orbital periods exceeding 100 years, the astrometric detection capabilities of Gaia's early data are substantial, particularly in systems with observed orbital phases favoring partial orbit measurement. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that Gaia's astrometry is capable of detecting partial orbits in approximately 70% of the systems, although this figure drops to around 30% when considering only the most reliable data.

This study aims to evaluate the influence of distinct single-point crossover and selection methods on the convergence of Genetic Algorithms in solving the 0/1 Knapsack Problem. A customized Genetic Algorithm was developed and tested on a range of challenging 0/1 Knapsack problems, including some provided by the original problem set. The results reveal that the genetic algorithm achieves faster convergence when operating on smaller populations, particularly when utilizing random selection methods. Conversely, traditional selection methods tend to yield better results when operating with larger population sizes.

This paper presents a proof of the $L^2$ estimates for a family of trilinear oscillatory operators, originally proposed by Zhang, with a specific type of convolution. These operators, initially defined over finite domains, can then be extended to apply to infinite domains. We apply this $L^2$ estimate to a new type of pseudo-differential operator, known as the oscillatory system, which was described by Metrebiani et al.

We have developed a model based on the T5 architecture that surpasses current state-of-the-art performance in detecting hate speech by 1% on the Twitter HateXplain dataset and 2% on the MSCoco Hateful Memes dataset. Through fine-tuning the model on the combined HateXplain and Hateful Memes datasets, we achieved state-of-the-art performance with a competitive approach, yielding an F1 score of 92.14% and establishing a new benchmark.

Achieving accurate interactions for complex systems is a significant hurdle in quantum chemistry, particularly with the increasing use of machine learning. We investigate the possibility of leveraging the Quantum Monte Carlo method to develop accurate interactions, despite its limited scalability. Our approach involves breaking down the interaction into two parts: a straightforward, short-range potential and an intricate, complex potential. We use a short-range model to approximate the first component and a neural network to model the second. We also introduce a technique called 'bootstrapping' to enhance accuracy. We apply this method to a water molecule and find that the method is effective, particularly with a sufficient number of particles, although it may struggle with the intricacies of many-electron potentials.

The 2020 US presidential election saw an unprecedented level of false claims regarding the voting process, with many spreading misinformation about voting methods. To better comprehend this issue, we created a new dataset of statements claiming election deception, sourced from Twitter between April and November 2020. This dataset, known as VoterFraud2020, contains 4,000 analyzed tweets along with their corresponding labels, as well as 1,500 associated images and videos. To enhance the dataset's value, we also developed a tool called ElectoProxy, which generates plausible, fact-based counterarguments for each claim. Our hope is that this dataset will serve as a valuable resource for researchers studying misinformation and provide valuable insights into the voting process.

We have established the presence of generic emergences in the set of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the 2-torus for a particular class of cocycles. This result enables the conclusion that the closed vector field derived from the linearized flow on the tangent bundle is not complete. This vector field, on the connected component of the set of vector fields defined on the set of non-wandering points and having positive Lyapunov exponents, exhibits unbounded behavior and thus cannot be topologically embedded within the connected component. This finding offers a first concrete demonstration of emergent dynamics in the set of vector fields characterized by nonzero Lyapunov exponents.

Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) designed to generate reliable uncertainty estimates for tasks such as classification and regression. However, these estimates often lack clarity, and the methods used to improve clarity often come at the cost of accuracy for classification tasks. In this study, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a posterior encoding network (PEN) to directly capture the underlying distribution of BNN's posterior latent space. This method allows for the creation of tight confidence bounds while maintaining high classification accuracy, and can be easily integrated into existing BNNs without additional training requirements. The proposed technique is demonstrated to outperform existing methods in terms of classification accuracy and confidence bound tightness, and is further shown to be effective in more complex real-world datasets.

A mathematical model has been developed to describe the rate of electron transfer between two molecules at their energy equilibrium, according to the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory. This theory states that, when a thermally-averaged energy loss is small, transfer rates are inversely proportional to the square of such an energy loss. At higher temperatures, where thermal energy loss becomes insignificant, transfer rates are controlled by tunneling rates. However, a new approach to understanding this process involves a mathematical technique that takes into account both the thermal energy loss and tunneling effects without requiring any additional assumptions, unlike previous methods. This new approach has been successfully applied to a real-world example of electron transfer in a copper atom attached to a carbon nanotube.

This research introduces a novel method for designing trajectory-based control systems, incorporating both optimal boundary conditions and feedback control mechanisms, specifically tailored for nonlinear infinite-dimensional systems. The open-loop control prior to feedback implementation is modeled as an infinite-dimensional linear-quadratic optimal control problem, with corresponding costs and constraints. Following this, the feedback control system is reconfigured into an equivalent optimal control problem with finite-dimensional dynamics. The method effectively circumvents the traditional challenges of replicating infinite-dimensional state variables within finite-dimensional feedback control systems by utilizing the properties of semigroup operators. The resulting control system's convergence to the desired performance outcome is rigorously demonstrated. The method's efficacy is successfully demonstrated through its application to an example trajectory tracking problem for a semi-infinite rod.

A theoretical framework for the vast thermoelectric effect has been developed based on the magnon drag mechanism. This framework enables the prediction of the magnon drag coefficient in relation to the crystal structure and band parameters of the material. Using first-principles calculations, the framework has been applied to Ni$_{50}$Fe$_{50}$ thin films with the Cu$_{3}$Mn and Cu$_{3}$Au structures. The results show that the magnon drag coefficient in Ni$_{50}$Fe$_{50}$ films with the Cu$_{3}$Mn structure is significantly higher than that with the Cu$_{3}$Au structure. Furthermore, the potential of the Cu$_{3}$Mn structure in achieving a high-performance thermoelectric device is supported by the large difference between the Seebeck coefficient and the Hall coefficient, as well as the substantial magnitude of these coefficients.

The Perfect Sum problem, a longstanding challenge for general cases, has received limited attention despite its extensive use in combinatorial optimization and resource allocation. This issue arises when aiming to determine if a set of non-negative numbers can be combined to achieve a specific total value. Recent research has employed heuristic algorithms, but their effectiveness is restricted to specific problem subsets or solution spaces. This paper proposes a novel probabilistic method to address the Perfect Sum problem. This approach involves a linear programming formulation that is solved by iteratively relaxing the constraints. We demonstrate that our probabilistic method exhibits superior efficiency and accuracy compared to existing heuristic algorithms, particularly for large random datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this method is highly effective in identifying perfect sums for specific problem instances.

This research involves calculating specific elements of elevated order in finite fields, determined by non-trivial multiplicative subgroups. A particular emphasis is placed on finite fields, denoted by $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$, defined by non-trivial irreducible polynomials. Research findings indicate that the elements of elevated order in these fields predominantly take the form of a binomial, where the coefficient originates from a specific subset within the field, thereby providing a distinct characteristic for these elements. Additionally, the study explores the existence and uniqueness of such binomials in specific finite fields, including those defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

Formal methods, such as model checking, enable the comprehensive analysis of complex systems by evaluating their dynamic behavior. The model checking process typically requires a formal description of the system in question. Our research focuses on developing a framework that integrates the model checking tool UPPAAL with popular programming languages like Java and C++ for in-depth source code analysis.

A new class of materials known as metasurfaces holds the potential to significantly improve imaging technology. To unlock this possibility, precise control of their electromagnetic properties across the entire visible spectrum is necessary, a task that has proven difficult to achieve. This research presents a novel, multi-step process for creating metasurfaces that can selectively focus light on various colors. By first using a technique called nanoreplica molding to mass-produce metasurfaces with uniform properties, these surfaces are then analyzed using a unique algorithm that compresses and refines data, identifying areas where adjustments are needed. This method, combined with the use of a specialized nanofabrication technique, enables the production of metasurfaces capable of resolving distinct colors with a high level of accuracy, and may have implications for the development of metasurfaces with advanced functions such as those that manipulate light polarizations.

The behavior of highly excited atoms under the influence of extremely strong, two-color laser fields has been examined. By manipulating the laser field parameters, specific spectral lines from the atoms can be selectively brought into resonance with the laser frequency, resulting in unique spectral shifts. These shifts can occur at both the peak and in between the peak of the laser frequency, and our research has identified and measured these shifts in the spectral emissions of two specific atoms under varying laser conditions. Furthermore, our study reveals that these spectral lines are not only shifted in intensity but also show altered widths and orientations, allowing for the effective control of these emission characteristics through adjustment of the laser parameters.

Image blending techniques have significantly advanced in producing high-quality results. However, we hypothesize that current methods are limited by prioritizing image details over semantic meaning, leading to unsatisfactory outcomes when combining images with distinct semantic meanings. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that enables seamless image blending by mapping semantic structures between images. Our method involves transforming one image into the style of the other while maintaining the original's semantic meaning in its transformed version. By merging the transformed image with the original, we can generate a new image that seamlessly integrates the semantic meanings of its predecessors, thus achieving a more effective image blend. Our approach is built on the concept of diffusion-based generative models and utilizes a novel semantic-aware loss function to ensure the integrity of image details and the preservation of semantic meaning. Our method has been tested on a range of image blending scenarios and has demonstrated substantial improvements in producing high-quality results.

The patterns of gene expression are represented as time series data in which each gene is associated with a sequence of noisy values. These noisy values result from a complex process driven by the cell's metabolic activity, and although the underlying dynamics are not fully understood, it's possible to extract relevant information from the resulting stochastic trajectories. This research presents a novel method for identifying essential features in gene trajectories. The proposed approach is based on a combination of statistical methods and data compression techniques, and it's designed to uncover hidden patterns in both the temporal and spatial dimensions of gene expression. The developed tool is capable of analyzing gene sequences and classifying their expression patterns. This is demonstrated through the application of the method to a specific type of cellular data, and the resulting classifications are found to accurately reflect known patterns of cell differentiation during human development.

A novel approach to semi-supervised learning is proposed, which integrates the capabilities of both unsupervised and supervised methods. The proposed framework is highly adaptable and not limited to a specific algorithm, thereby allowing for seamless application across various data analysis techniques. The primary goal is to develop a system that can accurately predict continuous target values and capture the underlying patterns in the data feature space. A comprehensive theoretical framework is formulated to analyze the proposed method under the assumption of the Strong Mixtures Condition, which guarantees tight generalization bounds for the method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed framework can effectively utilize data augmentation to enhance its performance and even address multi-class classification problems with multiple binary labels. The proposed method is validated through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its potential for achieving high-quality results.

In the quantum circuit-based variational quantum eigensolver, we observe that increasing the number of layers leads to significant fluctuations in the training fidelity, ultimately resulting in a saturated region where further progress seems impossible. By focusing on the one-qubit Pauli X operator as a target to understand these dynamics, we delve into the effects of the target state's structure and the initial qubit state distribution on the saturation point. Our analysis reveals that training becomes challenging when the target state's amplitude diminishes, measured by the 1-norm. Notably, we find that using a maximally mixed initial state allows for smooth convergence, whereas other initial states lead to the characteristic 'wandering' of the training fidelity by small amounts at regular intervals.

The growing use of multi-source data has led to the increasing importance of multi-source re-identification, a problem that goes beyond traditional database re-identification issues. In this research, we delve into the specific case of re-identifying individuals from multiple databases, examining the essential requirements for a re-identification attack to be feasible. We then introduce a new statistical model that accurately predicts the likelihood of identifying individuals across sources, and use real-world datasets to demonstrate the model's validity. Additionally, our study reveals that the probability of identifying individuals is influenced by how data is distributed, highlighting the need for careful consideration in multi-source data analysis.

To address the "data challenge" in modern power system development, this study introduces a novel approach to data-driven time series analysis. It leverages a fully automated, data-driven method to reconstruct time series based on its initial segment using the EEKF-IR (Extended Extended Kalman Filter-based Incremental Reconstruction) algorithm. This method enables the use of an EKF for both initial parameter estimation and real-time filtering of future data. Our approach allows for the effective analysis of short and long-term time series data, which is crucial for the research of modern power systems. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have incorporated our method into PyIR, a Python package for data-driven time series analysis.

This research examines the algorithm $A(\cdot)$, which uses an infinitesimal perturbation to approximate a unique solution $u$ of a variational inequality problem defined on a real, bounded convex set $C$. The algorithm $A(\cdot)$ is assumed to operate randomly within any set $R$ with $A(R)$ also being within $R$. The solution $u$ is defined such that for any set $S$ containing $u$, there is a subsequence of $u_n$ within $A(nu_n)$ with a limit point in $u$. The solution $u$ is the only point in $C$ satisfying this condition, with this uniqueness established under the assumption of a specific property in the algorithm's behavior.

This study focuses on the relationship between crosscuts in a genus 2, 3, and 4 hyperbolic Riemann surface, and Fuchsian groups with signature (0; g, g, r, r). By applying the concept of isoxial groups, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a specified non-separating crosscut to be present, and provide a straightforward testable criterion for another non-separating crosscut. Additionally, we investigate the occurrence of a specified type of separating crosscut under certain conditions, and provide an example illustrating our findings.

A search for Lepton Flavour Violation (LFV) occurred through the $\Upsilon(3S)$ decay to $e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$. The investigation was carried out at the BEPC electron-positron collider, utilizing the BESIII detector. A  $5.0\sigma$ signal for the desired decay was detected, and the branching ratio for $e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ was measured at $(2.15\pm0.96\pm0.18)\times10^{-6}$. This branching ratio is in line with predictions from the Standard Model and represents the first direct upper limit for the $\Upsilon(3S)$ to $e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ transition probability.

Pd$_3$P$_2$(S,Se)$_8$ compounds have garnered significant interest for their unique flat energy bands and the presence of a topological semimetal phase. By applying hydrostatic pressure, researchers observed a unique transformation where the topological semimetal transitions into a superconducting state at approximately 1 GPa, with a critical pressure (1.5 GPa) significantly lower than previously observed in other flat-band compounds. The superconducting critical temperature increases with pressure, reaching 2.5 K at 3 GPa, or double its value at ambient conditions. Notably, the superconducting critical temperature grows more slowly with pressure compared to other systems, suggesting a complex interplay between the emergence of superconductivity and the electronic structure of the compound. These findings offer new insights into the relationship between flat-band topology and superconductivity.

We have developed a method for retrieving black hole data using the Jackiw Teitelboim theory, which involves calculating the energy spectrum and identifying specific energy modes corresponding to the initial and final states of the black hole. In this process, we must account for the backreaction on the black hole geometry, resulting from the emission or absorption of vast numbers of quanta with arbitrarily low energy. A key challenge arises from the necessity to evaluate path integrals that depend on complex actions with a large number of variables, a problem that becomes exponentially complicated. To address this issue, we have devised a simplified approach that enables us to reduce the number of variables and demonstrate that the resulting action is a good approximation to the original path integral. This method allows us to recover the energy of the black hole by summing the energy modes within a specific range, up to sub-exponential corrections in the logarithm of the inverse energy. Furthermore, we have applied this approach to the problem of recovering a BTZ black hole data by emitting or absorbing a finite number of quanta with high energy. In this case, we have been able to recover the energy of the black hole up to polynomial corrections in the logarithm of the energy.

The neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) method has become a prominent deep learning technique for modeling time series data and solving differential equations. However, real-world data often features irregular time gaps and measurement inaccuracies, which have been largely overlooked in existing research. Our study examines the impact of these two forms of data irregularity on neural ODEs, revealing significant performance degradation. To address this issue, we introduce a comprehensive method combining resampling, smoothing, and forward-sampling strategies to enhance neural ODEs' robustness to noisy data. Our experiments using both simulated and actual data validate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving superior results for neural ODEs.

The Transformer architecture has achieved remarkable success in vision and language tasks, yet its application to vision-serve navigation is hindered by a significant limitation. Specifically, the Transformer model relies heavily on context from nearby tokens, making it difficult to effectively utilize distant context, particularly when navigating through complex environments with numerous objects. To address this issue, we present a novel approach called Object Recall Transformer, which incorporates an efficient object recall mechanism to enhance the recall of distant object context. By enabling the model to dynamically select and recall relevant objects based on the current viewpoint and environment layout, the object recall module significantly boosts the model's recall of distant context. Our experiments on two large-scale navigation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method, and further analysis reveals that the object recall module plays a crucial role in the model's performance.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of language model instruction meta learning (IML) in creating models that surpass the performance of both GPT-3 and large language models (LLMs) on various tasks. However, these models often fail to generalize well to real-world applications, particularly when faced with more complex scenarios. This paper delves into the generalization issues of IML models and identifies the root causes of these problems. We also introduces an optimization technique called OPT-IML, which aims to enhance the generalization of IML models during the pre-training phase. By utilizing multiple large language models as the backbone for IML, OPT-IML has the potential to improve the generalization of these models, as evidenced by its successful application in scaling GPT-3 to achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple task benchmarks.

This study examines how the social network features in Scratch, a popular learning environment for kids to learn programming, facilitate learning through Legitimate Peripheral Participation (LPP). By analyzing 100 accounts over 5 years, we discovered that social connections in Scratch are often short-lived, but users frequently engage with various groups and contribute to various projects, enabling them to participate in multiple LPP situations. We found that LAPP instances are influenced by the frequency and variety of a user's social interactions, including the roles they assume in different projects, and their involvement in specific discussion forums focused on particular project goals.

A perturbation theory is developed for a system consisting of electrons interacting with nuclei in the random phase approximation of the static Coulomb interaction, using the adiabatic connection of the transcorrelated electronic Hamiltonian. The resulting perturbation expansion is transformed into the uniform electron gas phase, where the RPA Coulomb potential is perturbed. The impact of the transcorrelation potential is considered by analyzing the density matrix of the Coulomb interaction in the uniform electron gas. The theory is applied to calculate the correlation energy of the random phase approximation, yielding an expression that is comparable to the random phase approximation of the Dirac-Kohn Hamiltonian.

To enhance the accuracy of estimating the covariance matrix of a Gaussian random field, we introduce a novel inflation method that incorporates site uncertainty. Our inflation approach utilizes the uncertainty of the field values at specific sites, quantified through their covariance matrix, to optimize the covariance matrix of the random field. By utilizing the Hessian matrix of the field, our inflation is grounded in optimal transportation principles. Notably, our inflation is physically plausible and respects the positive semi-definite property of the covariance matrix, even in the presence of site uncertainty. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our inflation in Gaussian process regression models over traditional maximum likelihood estimation methods, both in terms of numerical stability and accuracy.

The growing prevalence of sensitive data in various fields, particularly healthcare and finance, necessitates robust data privacy safeguards. However, the increasing volume and sensitivity of data poses significant challenges to both data protection and efficient processing. Consequently, developing effective solutions to these problems remains a pressing research endeavor. This study introduces an innovative safeguarding technique for private and distributed data known as Randomized Tensor Network Decomposition (RTND). It leverages the properties of the low-rank tensor approximation to efficiently decompose data into smaller, distributed components, thereby reducing the burden of data processing. We further extend this approach by proposing Dispersed Tensor Network Computation (DTNC), a method for distributed matrix-vector multiplication that disperses computation across multiple nodes, significantly reducing communication costs without compromising data security. Our approach offers a simple yet efficient solution for both data decomposition and computation, thereby simplifying the data processing pipeline and minimizing the risks associated with data breaches. We evaluate the performance of RTND and DTNC through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, demonstrating their superiority over existing methods in terms of both efficiency and security.

To effectively transfer learning from a simulator to real-world settings, robots need to safely navigate their environments, which requires the use of multiple control policies to minimize the risk of catastrophic events. We present SafeAPT, a simulation-based learning technique, which uses diverse policies to ensure safe and efficient transfer. SafeAPT employs a hierarchical risk assessment method to identify potential dangers and incorporates a dynamic risk management system, allowing the robot to minimize harm while achieving its objectives. By leveraging the benefits of both exploration and safety, SafeAPT achieves safe robot operation. We tested SafeAPT in multiple, complex scenarios, including a robotic arm's ability to grasp and manipulate objects and a self-driving car's capacity to navigate real-world settings. The results demonstrate that SafeAPT successfully ensures safe robot operation.

The nature of jets in both radio galaxies and blazars remains a fundamental enigma in modern astrophysics. While significant progress has been made in understanding the properties of jet plasma and the impact of relativistic motion along their length, there is still considerable uncertainty regarding the formation of jets and their development over time. Through a combination of radio and X-ray observations, along with the application of advanced techniques such as wide-band radio imaging and high-resolution X-ray imaging, we have the opportunity to gain insight into the structure and evolution of jets and their relationship to black hole growth and galaxy evolution. In this review, we will first examine the characteristics of jets in radio galaxies and blazars, before discussing the findings from recent, multi-wavelength studies of these fascinating objects.

This research addresses a time-inconsistent time-varying linear model, where optimal outcomes are defined by time-averaged, recursive expectations. To maintain stationarity, the model includes time-version effects. New results on sieve sieving have been developed to handle time-inconsistency, enabling efficient estimation. Additionally, the research introduces a two-stage approach to handle large models with many parameters, allowing for more precise inference. Simulation results and an analysis of inflation and GDP data validate this method.

The detection of objectionable language in written texts has become a pressing issue, requiring sophisticated techniques. A significant amount of research has focused on developing advanced methods for identifying and classifying objectionable language, particularly in the context of social media platforms. This study examines the effectiveness of cutting-edge neural network models in this field, including the BERT and XLM models, particularly their RoBERTa variant. Our findings demonstrate that the BERT and RoBERTa models exhibit exceptional performance, with the RoBERTa model achieving a high F1 score of 98.8% and a mean average precision of 99.4% on the Twitter dataset. This research contributes to the body of knowledge by presenting an in-depth analysis of the BERT and RoBERTa models in the context of objectionable language detection.

The brain's functional connectivity, a key aspect of its structure, is a complex phenomenon that is difficult to fully capture using traditional methods, limiting our understanding of the brain's neural pathways. This limitation makes it challenging to study the brain's dynamics and develop new treatments for neurological disorders. To overcome these challenges, we propose a data-driven approach that uses deep learning to discover functional connectivity patterns in neural systems. By analyzing neural spike train data from multiple brain regions, we can uncover the patterns and relationships between these patterns and the brain's underlying connectivity. This knowledge can then be used to study the brain's dynamics and develop new treatments for neurological disorders. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of brain function and improve treatment outcomes for neurological conditions.

Building on Wibisono and Stephens (2019), we apply the dissipativity theory of stochastic differential equations to a widely-used optimization method, Nesterov's Nesterov momentum. We obtain novel connections between its parameters and the convergence rate of the sequence, without relying on specific assumptions about the objective function. We then apply this framework to stochastic optimization problems, such as those involving average stochastic gradient descent, and derive new insights into the convergence rate of the underlying sequence under the condition L2 < μ3 / 2, in conjunction with the standard condition μ1 < μ2.

This research focuses on developing boundary treatments for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods when applied to hyperbolic systems with variable source terms, with an emphasis on stability analysis. By establishing a framework for numerical source terms, we utilize the discrete characteristic boundary conditions method to address the boundary issue. This method is further applied to the one-way wave equation model, where both numerical experiments and stability analysis are conducted.

Thin-film silicon solar cells hold great promise, but their absorption within the solar spectrum remains a challenge, particularly for ultrathin films that struggle to absorb light. A 3D photonic band gap back reflector has the potential to enhance absorption in thick and ultrathin Si solar cells. In this study, the light absorption within and beyond a Si slab was simulated using the FDTD method, revealing that the PBGBR could double the light absorbed within thin Si layers as thin as 50 nm, and significantly increase absorption in ultrathin films by preventing or greatly reducing transmission.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called credal valuation networks that integrates credal sets, an imprecise probability framework, with Bayesian valuation networks to develop artificial reasoning under uncertainty. Credal valuation networks expand on the traditional BNNs by allowing for imprecise probabilities within both node assessments and interconnection weights. This paper outlines the design principles of credal valuation networks, outlines a step-by-step calculation procedure, and verifies the accuracy of the approach through thorough testing. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of credal valuation networks by applying them to two distinct tasks: constructing a decision-making system, and identifying the structure of a causal network.

The task of Top-K recommendation involves identifying the most relevant items for a given target item based on their respective scores. To achieve this, a metric learning-based approach can be utilized, which aims to bring relevant items closer to the target and push non-relevant items away. However, traditional metric learning methods are often plagued by poor performance due to their reliance on a fixed margin, leading to issues such as subpar performance and inefficient training processes. To address these limitations, a novel method called Probabilistic Metric Learning with Adaptive Margin (PML-AM) has been developed, which incorporates a probabilistic distance loss function that dynamically adjusts its margin. This adaptive margin is determined by the similarity between the target and its relevant neighbors. By incorporating a noise perturbation technique, PML-AM can prevent the model from overfitting to non-relevant items. Empirical evidence gathered on multiple benchmark datasets confirms that PML-AM outperforms other leading methods in the field.

The behavior of quantum channels can be modeled using a stochastic evolution, 
where the system is in a specific state, interacting with an environment 
that adds noise to the system. Non-Markovian behavior occurs in these channels 
when future interactions with the environment affect past evolution. This paper 
investigates a specific type of non-Markovian behavior, which remains at a 
stable state under repeated interactions with the environment. We show that 
this type of non-Markovian behavior is long-lasting and not just a temporary 
phenomenon, and it is also present in channels that are unitary on average.

To address the issue of biased AI models, we have developed an innovative system that can identify and rectify biases in AI models through counterfactual reasoning. This approach involves identifying and addressing the root causes of bias within a dataset, specifically by pinpointing key features that contribute to biased decisions. By analyzing the effects of altering these pivotal features, known as counterfactuals, we can mitigate existing biases and ultimately improve the accuracy of the model. Additionally, we have created a framework that utilizes a genetic algorithm to optimize the selection of critical features and accelerate the counterfacing process. This technique has been successfully applied to real-world data, such as the COMPAS dataset, and has demonstrated its ability to significantly reduce bias while increasing the model's accuracy.

The field of robotics is witnessing a significant surge in the adoption of autonomous systems, driven by advancements in perception capabilities, communication, and decision-making. In this context, the development of autonomous systems heavily relies on the integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computer vision. For machine learning-based algorithms to be effective in real-world applications, they must be trained and evaluated using a substantial dataset of relevant examples. However, the creation of such datasets is labor-intensive and often specialized, resulting in a shortage of available resources. In an effort to address this issue, we present RoSmEEry, an open-source platform that simulates real-world environments to support the evaluation of semantic mapping algorithms. RoSmEEry leverages the capabilities of Gazebo and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping to provide a comprehensive platform for creating, visualizing, and assessing simulated environments. This platform enables researchers to easily integrate and evaluate semantic mapping algorithms, including those utilizing machine learning approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RoSmEEry by successfully integrating various learning-based algorithms within the SimPy system, allowing us to assess their performance in simulating real-world scenarios.

Rikudo is an NP-complete board placement game for two players. Starting with an initially configured board, two players take turns placing a single card at a time. Each card shares one connection with another, with either a straight or curved path linking them. A player wins by completing all card placements. Non-playing cards are removed due to conflicting paths with played cards. A winning strategy exists for at least one player unless a specific combination of cards results in a "Rikudo", rendering the game unwinnable for both players. In this study, the authors confirm Rikudo is an NP-complete problem, and additionally demonstrate that even restricted versions where a "Rikudo" is intentionally included, still maintain NP-completeness.

Optimal transport theory's ability to compare probability distributions makes it a valuable tool in various scientific and engineering fields. Its wide applications are grounded in a method for calculating the transport plan that minimizes the cost between two measures. This chapter focuses on the numerical solution of the optimal transport problem, aiming to provide an in-depth overview of available techniques and their respective complexities. We will examine the methods' strengths and weaknesses, highlighting the recent developments in OT's field and their potential impact on future research and development.

Ramanujan's paper from 1913 contains four key congruence properties related to the Ramanujan $\beta (d,n)$ for specific moduli $p$ that are the first primes in sequences. We'll investigate an underlying pattern utilizing the Hecke theory for automorphic forms, utilizing this approach to establish a general theorem that encapsulates all four main congruences mentioned earlier, thus providing insight into the deeper connection between Ramanujan's modular identities and Hecke groups.

We've conducted a detailed analysis of the Keck ESI spectrograph's high-resolution observations of eight gravitationally lensed quasars, which exhibit varying time delays with lensing distances. These time delays, combined with lens models derived from HST and Keck photometric data, have allowed us to investigate the effects of time delay calibration errors. We've also made new measurements of the redshifts of the lensing galaxies in five systems and confirmed previously known redshifts in three others. Our data reveal that the lensing galaxies' velocity dispersions range from 100 to 300 km/s and their redshifts span from 0.15 to 0.85. We've also identified a correlation between the lensing galaxies' velocity dispersions and their Einstein radius, which supports the idea that the deflection potential is directly proportional to the mass distribution. We've further estimated the masses of the lensing galaxies and found that their masses are in line with expectations based on the Tully-Fisher relation.

This paper introduces a novel approach to solve $q$-fractional differential equations over a time scale. By converting the equation into an integral equation using a Volterra-type solution, we obtain the underlying integral equation. Due to the complexities of time scale derivatives, direct application of the Redheffer variation of parameters formula is impractical, so we employ the Redheffer formula in conjunction with the Cauchy-type operator to transform the integral equation. This enables us to derive a Volterra-type integral equation, which is subsequently solved via the Resolvent method. Ultimately, we present three practical case studies to demonstrate the efficacy of this method.

The phonon Hall effect, discovered recently in n-type bismuth, has sparked significant interest in the field of solid-state physics. To better understand this phenomenon, we examine the theoretical framework underlying the phonon Hall effect and its topological characteristics. By analyzing the Berry phase factor in the phonon's reciprocal space, we find that it exhibits a non-zero phase, resulting in a non-zero topological Chern number. Consequently, the phonon state becomes topologically insulating, and the mechanism driving the phonon Hall effect can be identified as a topological phase transition. Additionally, our study reveals that the Berry phase factor in the real space is continuous and smooth, indicating that the phonon state becomes a topological insulator. Furthermore, the vanishing of the phonon Hall effect at low temperatures suggests that the phonon state is a topological insulator, consistent with the observed behavior in n-type bismuth.

Raman spectroscopy's capabilities can be enhanced by combining it with imaging, allowing for the detection of molecular structures at the cellular level. Nonetheless, the process of acquiring Raman spectra is time-consuming, thus limiting the speed at which images can be captured. Raman resonance imaging microscopy (RRIM) overcomes this limitation by utilizing time-correlated single photon counting, but its application is restricted to microscopic samples. To overcome this limitation, the Shifted Excitation Raman Differential Spectroscopy (SERDS) method has been developed, enabling the acquisition of Raman spectra without the need for time-correlated counting. Nevertheless, the method's inability to be applied to broad-field fluorescence microscopy and its sensitivity to variations in the laser's power have further limited its application. To overcome this limitation, the Nod and Shuffle Integration Method was developed, enabling the collection of Rasterscan Raman spectra at a rate of up to 1000 per second. The Nod and Shuffle technique utilizes the Nod and Shuttle method to rapidly collect Rasterscan images of the sample at a rate of up to 1000 images per second. The Nod and Shuffle integration method was then used to rapidly collect Rasterscan images of the sample at a rate of up to 1000 images per second. The Nod and Shuffle integration method was then used to rapidly collect Rasterscan images of the sample at a rate of up to 1000 images per second. The Nod and Shuffle integration method was
