This paper introduces a novel concept called matrix Fejér and Levin-Stechkin interpolations. This concept enables the development of a matrix invariant of a complex rectangular matrix $A$, which ranges between its numerical range and the norm of $A$. This inequality is applicable to both real and complex matrices $A$. Furthermore, the inequality can be extended to the case where $A$ is a function. Additionally, the paper discusses connections to the Schur complement, the Fejér and Stechkin inequalities, and provides a list of relevant open research questions.

We investigate the mean null energy condition on the event horizons of Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes that are evaporating due to quantum effects.  The mean condition is violated at the singularity that forms during evaporation, and this violation persists until just before the singularity is created.  Interestingly, the mean condition is restored as the black hole approaches its complete evaporation.  We have also calculated the mean energy flux passing through the event horizon.  This flux is found to be finite, despite the singularity and associated energy effects.  We have also explored the energy flux in the context of the weak energy condition.
In this paper, we will examine the dimensions of operators within a two-dimensional conformal field theory and discuss how to identify its universal characteristics from an algebraic perspective.

The 2nd edition of the ICS-CTM2 cybersecurity testing maturity model provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the effectiveness of testing for Industrial Control Systems. This updated model builds upon its predecessor by incorporating newly identified testing needs and a standardized approach to assessing existing testing methodologies. The ICS-CTM2 serves as a foundational structure for a future standardized cybersecurity testing framework tailored to this domain. This version of the ICS-CTM2 serves as a crucial resource for organizations striving to enhance their internal testing capabilities. The ICS-CTM2 model was developed through a collaborative effort with industry stakeholders at the 2022 S4 Securing Industrial Automation Conference in Munich, Germany.

In a scenario involving a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) task, each agent learns its strategy independently, which can result in inefficient policies. To address this issue, this paper introduces a new approach that involves agents coordinating their actions by taking into consideration the benefits and losses incurred by other agents at a given state. To calculate these benefits, agents use a greedy-based method that considers the future payoff as an investment in the current payoff. The proposed method is efficient, with computational complexity of O(N), where N represents the number of actions available at a given state. A new algorithm, called GB-MARL, incorporates the proposed method and is demonstrated to enhance cooperation among agents through its ability to coordinate with other agents at a given state. Experimental results confirm that GB-MARL outperforms existing methods in terms of cooperation, as measured by the average reward.

Research has shown that language models contain stereotypical biases, yet measuring these biases in real-world scenarios remains a pressing concern. To address this issue, we developed StereoSet - a dataset designed to evaluate biases in a more authentic setting. By incorporating context and conflicting information, StereoSet enables the assessment of stereotypical biases' impact on predicted attributes. Our experiments reveal that, despite their impressive performance on various tasks, pre-trained language models like BERT and RoBERTa still exhibit biases in line with prevalent social stereotypes when making categorical predictions. Moreover, we found that BERT exhibits a bias in favor of existing gender stereotypes when used for few-shot learning. These findings highlight the need for further research on the impact of stereotypical biases in language models and encourage the development of more effective debiasing techniques. The StereoSet dataset is available for download at https://github.com/lrashid2112/stero_set.

To maintain the stability of the power grid, precise control over power line tilts in manufacturing is crucial.  However, conventional methods that rely solely on ground-based measurements to determine how power line tilt interacts with environmental factors are inadequate due to the complexity of the relationship.  A new method uses a novel combination of sensors, artificial intelligence, and machine learning to directly measure the tilt of electrical components and improve prediction accuracy.  By leveraging this data, machine learning models can be trained to create accurate tilt simulations, which can then be used to create optimal control systems for distantly located manufacturing processes.  A new method called Off-Policy Learning is used to train these machine learning models without requiring real-time control actions, which can be particularly useful given the cost of implementing such a system.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the new method, we conducted experiments using real data from a recent pilot study of the new method's components, which showed that the Off-Policy Learning method can achieve a 50% reduction in mean squared error, which translates to a 75% reduction in control action.  A detailed analysis of the new method's performance and its limitations is also presented.

A comprehensive analysis of the CKM unitarity phase, denoted by $\gamma$, is presented by the LHCb collaboration, combining the results of two key studies. The first investigation involved a combination of two neutral B-meson decays, namely $B^0 \to \phi K^0_s$, $D^0 \to K^+ K^-/\pi^+ \pi^-$, and $B^0 \downarrow \to D^0 \pi^+\pi^-\) in conjunction with $D^0 \to \downarrow \overline{K}^0 K^+\pi^-$, utilizing full LHCb data sets. The second study integrated $B_s \to D^0 K^-\pi^+$ and $B_s \to D^0 \downarrow K^-\pi^+$ data, with the latter subject to specific flavor requirements, to yield an estimate of $\gamma$ in the $b$-flavored sector. The analysis is accompanied by a detailed examination of the sources of uncertainty and systematic errors. The findings indicate a value of $\gamma = (136^{+22}_{-18})^\circ$ for the first study and $\gamma = (79^{+18}__{-16})^\circ$ for the second; both results are expressed at 68% confidence level.

This note delves into the properties of a particular family of ellipsoids, specifically the $3\times 4$ ellipsoid family, which is notable for its complex symmetry and lack of real symmetry. We explore the geometric implications of complex conjugation and linear coordinate transformations on the ellipsoid's shape, as well as the conditions that allow for the emergence of real symmetry. Moreover, we demonstrate that the transformation required to attain real symmetry is always linear.

A platform for personal data trading has been conceptualized as a market where individuals sell and buy sensitive information, allowing them to negotiate terms and prices. However, the feasibility of such a platform remains uncertain due to potential concerns from users and legal and ethical implications. To address these questions, researchers conducted a survey and focus group to explore users' perceptions of this market, their data value, and their willingness to participate. The study found that individuals value their personal data but are cautious about sharing it, with the majority being unwilling to sell their data, except in cases of critical health issues and social media influence. The study also revealed that users lack awareness of the value of their data and the potential benefits of data sharing, and they prioritize privacy concerns above financial benefits. Based on these findings, researchers suggest that data market platforms may not be viable in the near future but can still serve a purpose in raising user awareness and informing data ethics policies.

In novel communication systems, Quicker-than-Nyquist (QTN) signaling schemes employ an extended symbol sequence for each information symbol, enabling a faster symbol rate than the Nyquist rate. This approach presents a new challenge for detecting the received symbols due to excess inter-symbol interference (ISI), which hinders the application of low-complexity soft decision decoding methods like soft sign decision and list sphere decoding. This paper proposes a deep learning-based framework for detecting the QTN symbols, incorporating a pre-distortion technique to reduce the ISI effects and a two-stage neural network designed to exploit the ISI-free features of the ISI-free symbols, thus enabling the use of list sphere decoding for faster-than-Nyquist signaling detection. Simulation results confirm the proposed method's ability to achieve a lower error rate for QTN signaling than existing detection methods.

We introduce order topology to effect algebras with weights and investigate the properties of both order topologies and finest Frink ideals within this context. Utilizing these findings, we then examine the order topology of both bounded and unbounded quantum effect algebras with weights in finite dimensional Hilbert spaces.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance in image classification tasks. Nevertheless, these models often rely on data augmentation techniques that introduce random transformations to images, which can result in irrelevant information being fed into convolutional neural networks (CNNs). To address this issue, we introduce SaliencyMix, a data augmentation technique that utilizes saliency maps to mask unimportant areas and apply random transformations to preserved regions. By doing so, SaliencyMix enables the creation of more informative data augmentations that enhance model generalizability. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K datasets demonstrate that SaliencyMix outperforms traditional methods, with improvements in accuracy and learning speed. Furthermore, SaliencyMix offers a more efficient learning process, which can accelerate training by up to 2.5 times. The accompanying code is available for public use.

We provide a characterization of left or right $L_\infty$-cyclic or weakly cyclic operators on the Hilbert space through an equivalent description of traceable operators, which aligns with the definition given by relative continuous Fourier analysis on the infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebra.

A new gravitational theory, known as Altered Gravity, aims to address the discrepancy between the observed behavior of large-scale structures and the predictions of General Relativity. By incorporating a single additional parameter, Altered Gravity can be distinguished from Horndeski theory. Intrinsic galaxy alignment can be used to test this theory, as it is sensitive to the gravitational potential. By measuring the 3D alignment of galaxies, it can provide a new way to test Altered Gravity. In this study, we propose a new method to measure intrinsic galaxy alignment and demonstrate its effectiveness in distinguishing between Altered Gravity and General Relativity. We also discuss the potential for future surveys to use both intrinsic galaxy alignment and shear to make more precise distinctions between these theories.

In systems of highly structured particles, conventional Navier-Stokes rheology no longer applies due to non-constant deformation and rotation. This study focuses on the fluid-like behavior of specific self-healing gels formed from star polymers. Our findings reveal that these gels exhibit non-traditional rheology characterized by time-independent deformations and rotation, which cannot be predicted by conventional rheology models. We developed a micro-mechanics framework that accurately models large-scale gels' macroscopic rheological properties, which cannot be predicted by conventional rheology models. This new framework successfully predicts the unique non-stationary rheology of gels under oscillation and shear, providing valuable insights into the mechanical characteristics of structural gels.

The thermal analysis of metallic nanoparticles has been extensively studied using numerical models, particularly focusing on the phase change and decomposition of individual particles, to gain insight into their microscopic characteristics. However, these models are often limited by the use of constant temperature and lack the ability to incorporate experimental data directly. In this research, a more advanced thermal model, based on the molecular dynamics (MD) method, was developed to simulate the melting of gold nanoparticles under scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) conditions. The model was further enhanced by the incorporation of electron beam-induced heat and was able to characterise the electron beam's impact on the particles, as supported by experimental findings. The developed simulation approach can be applied to other electron beam analysis techniques and scanning probe microscopy methods, as well as be extended to other types of nanoparticles, including insulating and semiconductor materials.

This is the initial part of a series that develops and applies a general formulation of a splitting theorem for operators that have potential. It also presents a general formulation of a bifurcation theorem for operators that have potential. Initially, we develop a methodical approach to prove the existence of solutions for operators that have constraints and conditions on the variable, assuming that these solutions exist under the condition that the variable's range is infinite. We then derive a method to approximate the solution of operator equations when the variable's range is infinite, provided that the solution exists. Additionally, we establish a method to prove the existence of solutions for operators that have constraints and conditions on the variable, provided that the variable's range is infinite, assuming that these solutions exist under specific conditions on the variable's range. We also derive a method to prove the existence of solutions for operators that have constraints and conditions on the variable, provided that the variable's range is infinite, and show that these solutions exist even if the variable's range is infinite. We use this method to prove the existence of solutions for operator equations when the variable's range is infinite, provided that the solution exists even if the variable's range is infinite.

The concept of taste tasting, or "how it tastes," is a subjective and highly personal experience, influenced by individual preferences and dislikes. As a result, it's challenging for people to accurately convey their subjective perceptions of a food's taste. This research introduces an innovative method for structuring the flavor profile of food using a three-part tetrahedron structure, which takes into account sweet, salty, bitter, and acidic flavors. By applying this model to the perception of salted strawberries, researchers found that the taste of this unique combination of flavors cannot be captured through its four basic taste characteristics alone.
We derive three new identities for the (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials.

Estimating the long-term effects of treatment on health outcomes is crucial in medical research.  However, this task is complicated by confounding variables and missing data.  To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning approach that integrates causal inference and missing data imputation.  A new policy is trained to mimic patients' real behavior, while a target policy is designed to estimate long-term treatment effects.  By iteratively imputing missing data and updating policies, the proposed method is shown to improve imputation and achieve consistent policy convergence.  Simulation studies and real-world data analysis have demonstrated the proposed method's superior performance compared to other approaches.

In research, identifying the causes of diseases is essential to develop effective treatments, which involves investigating the effects of certain factors on the development of diseases. However, studies involving case-control research often rely on data that includes bias stemming from various sources such as differential exposure, differential susceptibility, and selective participation, which can result in biased estimates of disease risk factors. To address this issue, researchers typically adjust for confounding factors using marginal structural models, which account for counterfactuals. However, studies involving selective exposure and bias also require a different approach. To address this, researchers have developed a method to measure selective memory, which is the difference in exposure distribution between cases and controls, and have developed a method to estimate disease risk factors while considering selective memory. This new method can be used in studies involving case-control research, and it can be applied to both discrete and continuous data sets.

Generative models can be viewed as complex data compression methods, and their training can be considered as reducing data variability. Autoencoders, which combine a compressor with a decoder, can be trained using the reconstruction loss in conjunction with the entropy of the compressed data. Traditionally, the compressor is designed with specific architectures in mind, leading to difficulties in assessing the influence of reconstruction loss on entropy. To address this, we suggest evaluating the quality of a compressor by examining the entropy of its output rather than relying on the reconstruction loss. We propose a straightforward method to achieve this by transforming the data into a suitable space for evaluation. Furthermore, we propose using reversible layers, which allow for exact calculation of the entropy. Our experiments demonstrate that focusing on entropy leads to improved results in terms of both reconstruction and data compression.

The concept of "smart" has become a prominent descriptor for modern societies. In response, numerous research initiatives have been established to explore the intricate network connecting cities to their inhabitants and their functioning parts. The goal of these studies is to create an in-depth understanding of the city's structure, allowing for the identification of potential issues and areas for improvement. This research model, centered on the city's status and progress, is crucial for its effective management. The main objective of this research paper is to present a data analysis and visualization method that helps scientists and policymakers make informed decisions regarding smart city development. By focusing on attribute correlation, this method enables the exploration of underlying relationships within the data, allowing for the discovery of meaningful and insightful patterns. The resulting output is then transformed into a visually appealing format using various visualization techniques, providing a clear and structured basis for further smart city research. In this research, we applied our method to the City Dataset, consisting of 1,500 city data points, to demonstrate its effectiveness.

This study introduces and assesses algebraic multigroind preconditioners for a low-order HDG discretization of two-dimensional reaction-diffusion problems and generalized Stokes equations. We examine two approaches: a novel recursive hierarchical basis technique and a block thresholding method applied to the matrix's off-diagonal elements. These preconditioners are effective in practice and significantly reduce solution time for single-field reaction-diffusion problems and two-field generalized Stokes problems compared to direct solvers, with an added benefit of the second preconditioner in achieving faster convergence rates.

Missing data in medical studies can lead to biased results, and sensitivity assessments are crucial to gauge the reliability of missing data analyses. Bayesian methods for handling missing data have gained attention in recent years, and this paper explores the application of Bayesian sensitivity assessments in missing data analyses. We introduce a Bayesian method grounded on the E-value framework to evaluate the reliability of missing data analyses. The proposed approach is illustrated through a sensitivity analysis of a large multicenter prostate cancer trial dataset, and the results demonstrate that a Bayesian multiple imputation analysis yields reliable inferences, whereas a frequentist analysis with multiple imputation fails to do so, thus highlighting the importance of Bayesian sensitivity assessments in missing data analyses.

In crossover trials where multiple missingness variables are involved, a single missing data analysis approach is unfeasible. To address this, multiple analysis strategies are applied to each endpoint and the results combined based on their statistical significance. A probability-based approach is then used to estimate the overall treatment effect by calculating a weighted average of individual analyses' point estimates and their corresponding standard errors. This methodological paper discusses the advantages and disadvantages of this approach and its optimal utilization. A simulation study was conducted to compare different analysis strategies, which showed that the probability-based approach provides type I error rates closest to the desired significance level and that point estimates and standard error values are accurately represented. A real-world example from a crossover study on the effects of different fish oil doses on triglyceride levels is also presented.

We define and explore the concepts of $L$-coherent frameworks and $L$-associative frameworks for categories, and demonstrate that the former corresponds to the existence of an associahedron in cohomology, providing a geometric interpretation of the Maurer-Lusztig cohomology tree. Furthermore, $L$-coherent frameworks are shown to be equivalent to $L$-associative frameworks under certain conditions, and we establish that the Priddy green homology symmetries of the Stasheff $K$-associahedron are root systems.

As the amount of data stored in memory continues to increase, DRAM, with its capacity for high-speed and low power consumption, remains the go-to memory technology.  However, the complexity of the DRAM interface has hindered the development of in-DRAM optimizations.  To address this limitation, we propose the CODIC framework, which enables the creation of customized in-DRAM solutions through a user-friendly programming interface.  CODIC's design builds on existing DRAM infrastructure, and its architecture is adaptable to various DRAM chips.  The framework's core components include a modular compiler, a simulator, and a hardware-enabling tool.  By utilizing CODIC, developers can create innovative in-DRAM solutions that significantly enhance memory performance, energy efficiency, and fault tolerance.  Furthermore, CODIC's modular design makes it easily extensible to other memory technologies, effectively turning DRAM into a programmable platform.

This is the second installment in a series exploring the intersection of functional programming and network research and development. As networks continue to virtualize and evolve, ensuring efficient management and coordination of resources becomes increasingly crucial. In this paper, we delve into the concept of virtualization and its implications for network management and development. We examine the role of functional programming in network design and its potential to inform the future of network research and pave the way for new applications and models.

To assess the performance of superconducting quantum processors, we've created a comprehensive evaluation framework centered on quantum error correction. Our approach is grounded in the toric code, which is implemented using two distinct methodologies: the first employs a combination of single-qubit and multi-qubit operations to replicate a logical qubit, while the second relies on single-qubit operations within a multi-qubit code. By developing a universal quantum circuit compiler, we've streamlined the process of translating logical operations and their error rates into physical implementations. Furthermore, we've successfully applied our framework to simulate complex scenarios, such as the execution of quantum algorithms within noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices and the implementation of quantum gate fidelities within such devices.

A key aspect of conducting modern astronomical research involves combining and operating a wide range of sophisticated instruments across multiple sites. To address this need, the OPUS system offers a standardized system for managing tasks, which can handle and integrate complex data products, such as large data sets, images, and virtual observatory objects. To provide additional flexibility, OPUS also supports the execution of external commands and tasks, which can facilitate integration with other tools. By adhering to established standards like SCS and PI, the system ensures seamless integration with existing observatory software and hardware. Additionally, OPUS is fully compliant with standards like PI, SCS, and WCS to ensure interoperability and accurate data processing. Furthermore, the system is capable of creating new, custom tasks dynamically, which can facilitate the processing of unstructured data sets. To demonstrate the system's capabilities, we outline its application in various astronomical domains, including the operation of imaging cameras, spectrographs, and data sets.

This study introduces an innovative approach to education through a digital game-based learning method focused on complex wireless networks. A novel game has been developed, which not only teaches students about network behavior but also allows them to simulate and experiment with network management decisions, fostering practical application skills. The game's potential to enhance education is supported by a pilot study, which yielded positive results from a moderate sample size of 76 students.

The widely accepted ozone-proximity indicator has been used to identify terrestrial exoplanets with atmospheres similar to Earth's, but it may not be reliable in certain cases. This method assumes a direct correlation between molecular oxygen and ozone, but this relationship can be affected by factors such as the presence of reduced species, UV shielding, and non-photolysis ozone sources. To understand the ozone-O2 relationship better, we conducted a study using Earth's atmosphere as a model to examine how variations in O2 are related to ozone. We found that the slope of the ozone-O2 relationship can be significantly influenced by the O2 mixing ratio, particularly when it is low, and that the relationship can be affected by factors that modify the O2 mixing ratio, such as the presence of reduced species or non-photolysis ozone sources. We also found that the slope of the ozone-O2 relationship can be affected by factors that modify ozone abundance, such as the presence of non-photolysis ozone sources. These factors can cause the slope to decrease by up to 50% and even become negative. We propose that the slope of the ozone-O2 relationship can be used to infer the presence of reduced species or non-photolysis ozone sources in a planet's atmosphere.

The quantum Hall effect's equivalent on a 3D lattice, characterized by a periodic magnetic field, displays unusual nonequilibrium properties when driven by a uniform electric field. This results in the emergence of persistent surface currents that are shielded from the driving force. This phenomenon is captured by a hydrodynamic model that accounts for the Larmor spin motion, offering a basic description of the system's behavior. The model's predictions are supported by numerical simulations.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation have led to the development of multilingual neural machine interpretation (MNMI) models, which can translate medical text into concise, interpretable concepts across multiple domains. However, these models often struggle with domain mismatch, particularly in scenarios where the test data significantly diverges from the training data in terms of statistical and distributional properties. To address this challenge, our research explores the effectiveness of domain-adapted MNMI, where the model is initially trained on data from a specific domain (source domain) and then fine-tuned using data from another domain (target domain). Our experiments demonstrate that domain-adapted MNMI can substantially enhance the model's performance, exemplified through its application in translating clinical notes from the NoteBank domain into medical concepts using MedCyclopedic.

A system consisting of non-extensive electrons, positively charged dust, and non-extensive ions is used to investigate the formation of altered-ion-acoustic waves. The influence of various physical factors such as non-extensivity, non-thermal electrons, and warm ions on the properties of these waves is analyzed. The findings indicate that the wave speed and its propagation are significantly affected by these factors. The wave speed is found to increase with increasing non-extensivity and background dust concentration. The wave's stability is also observed to increase with an enhancement in these factors. The wave can propagate in both directions in the presence of warm ions, but can only propagate in one direction in the absence of warm ions. The wave can propagate in both directions in the presence of non-extensivity, but can only propagate in one direction in the absence of non-extensivity. The wave's properties are found to be similar to those in the presence of non-thermal electrons. The presence of non-thermal electrons is found to have a significant effect on the wave's properties. The wave's properties are found to be altered by the concentration of warm ions, with the wave's speed and propagation being reduced in the presence of warm ions. The presence of warm ions and non-extensivity is found to have a significant effect on the wave's properties.

In a variety of natural language processing tasks, such as question answering, text summarization, and question classification, a crucial step is retrieving relevant text units. For multi-lingual retrieval, especially when dealing with an abundance of text data, the goal is to efficiently process a query across various languages, like English and German, without sacrificing accuracy. A common approach to this is to utilize sentence embeddings and measure the distance between these embeddings to rank search results. In this work, we propose an unsupervised method to generate these sentence embeddings by utilizing a pre-trained language model and then fine-tuning it for the retrieval task. Our method includes a novel technique to train the model on the query and surrounding context, thereby improving the semantic alignment between the two. Our experimental results on the DeEn dataset show that our approach outperforms existing methods, including those using monolingual and multi-lingual pre-trained models.

Multimodal learning, which combines information from various data types, is an area of interest, and recent advancements have shown that incorporating multiple modalities can enhance predictive accuracy. However, these methods often overlook the unique characteristics of each modality and fail to account for potential biases. This research presents a new method, Prototypical Modal Adjustment for Multimodal Learning (PMR), which utilizes prototypical networks to identify and account for modality-specific biases. By adjusting the representation of each modality based on a prototype that captures the common ground among all modalities, the approach enables more accurate and diverse representations. These refined representations are then combined to form the final predictive outcome. Experimental evaluations on diverse datasets have consistently shown that our proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

In this scenario, we develop and examine vector models of transport theory as initially proposed by Lev Landau. The application of the Landau frame allows for a clear, direct relationship between the model's dynamics and the characteristics of its underlying fields. When compared to earlier models based on the Nambu-Guralnik-Higuchi construction, which utilized the Goldstone boson only, our proposed model incorporates the vector sector as actively contributing entities. The resulting theory exhibits a more intricate dynamics, with electromagnetic interactions and Chern-Simons terms playing significant roles. The vector meson mass serves as a dynamic variable, influenced by the transport equations. An explicit example, built upon the hidden local symmetry model of QCD, demonstrates the emergence of the transport theory from the effective action. The resulting theory exhibits a range of novel features, including the potential for the vector meson mass to decrease as the system evolves.

This research introduces a new method that combines feed-forward and recurrent networks within the tensor-train architecture to improve the efficiency of spoken command recognition systems. By integrating these components, the model can capture both time-dependent and global patterns in audio data. We evaluated the approach using a spoken digit recognition task and found that it outperformed a standard feed-forward model, yielding an accuracy of 12.6% under time-shift conditions.

The two established master equation frameworks for open quantum systems - the Lindblad approach and the stochastic Schrödinger approach - have distinct advantages and disadvantages. In particular, the Lindblad approach offers clear physical interpretations of dissipation but is limited in its ability to generate position-space trajectories, whereas the Schrödinger approach provides a deeper mathematical structure but lacks a clear physical interpretation of dissipation. By demonstrating the equivalence of these formulations despite differing forms, we can now create a direct link between the physical dissipation mechanisms and the resulting trajectories. This has been achieved through the development of a new class of jump equations that can be used to model the evolution of these systems. As a result, we can now create a variety of non-Markovian jump trajectories that accurately reflect the behavior of these systems.

This study explores the geometric effects of plasmonic aluminum nanoparticles on silicon thin-film solar cells. We investigate how varying the nanoparticles' aspect ratio affects optical absorption in different concentrations of nanoparticles, ranging from 10% to 30%. By examining the nanoparticles' absorption spectra, we determine the relevant localized surface plasmon resonance and analyze its impact on optical absorption. Our findings reveal that increasing the nanoparticles' aspect ratio leads to a shift in the LSPR wavelength towards the solar cell's absorption band, thereby enhancing optical absorption. This discovery suggests that nanoparticles with a higher aspect ratio can serve as an efficient means to improve solar cell performance.

The study of descriptive complexity in database theory, specifically the analysis of first-order logic (FO) over finite structures through Datalog, has been a long-standing problem. The challenge lies in developing a general framework that can capture all functions expressible in FO without relying on non-elementary constructs, such as universal quantification and existential quantification combined with an enumeration construct. Building on the work of Freyd, Saini, and Simpson, researchers have explored a new logic called FSIS, designed to capture a key subset of FO functions. The current study extends this work by developing a more comprehensive logic, FSICS, which incorporates an additional choice operator and demonstrates the ability to capture a broader range of FO functions, specifically PTIME. The development of FSICS also builds upon existing FSIS-based logic frameworks, specifically the logics of Chlebus and of Worrell, Bloom, Hirschler, and Kolaitis.

LSTM deep learning networks have become a leading approach for handling time-dependent data, and are increasingly used in video classification tasks. However, these networks face significant challenges related to their size and complexity, particularly when dealing with large video datasets. To address this, we propose a novel co-design method that optimizes algorithmic and hardware components for LSTM networks. By applying Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition, we break down complex LSTM weight tensors into smaller, more manageable components that can be processed more efficiently. This approach can be integrated into hardware using a co-design framework, which enables the generation of customized hardware accelerators. These accelerators significantly reduce the computational overhead associated with HTD, allowing for faster video classification results. In comparison to existing hardware accelerators, our proposed method achieves notable improvements in energy efficiency, achieving a 2.45x reduction in energy consumption and a 1.76x increase in classification accuracy.

The MAVLink protocol, used by the ArduPilot and PX4 projects, is a widely used standard for unmanned aerial systems (UAS). However, its lack of security implementation makes it vulnerable to attacks. A recent study revealed several critical security weaknesses in the protocol, including the potential for remote code execution and data injection attacks. These vulnerabilities could compromise the security of UAS and put users' lives at risk. This paper proposes MAVSec, a secure version of the MAVSEC protocol, designed to protect against existing and potential attacks. By modifying the MAVLink protocol, MAVSec enhances its security, and its proposed cryptographic mechanisms ensure the confidentiality and authenticity of commands and responses. The feasibility of MAVSec has been demonstrated in practice through a successful integration with the ArduPilot autopilot, and its performance has been evaluated to ensure minimal overhead.

Distributed systems, such as data centers, edge networks, and IoT devices, offer a natural space for investigating complex, dynamic, and decentralized network behaviors in a non-coordinated manner.  In this research, a new tool called Kollaps is designed to simulate the collapse of a decentralized network into a simple network structure.  Kollaps is a decentralized network emulator that uses a user-defined network topology, basic computing nodes, and a minimal set of decentralized control protocols to replicate the behavior of a complex, dynamic network.  Kollaps is a versatile tool that can be used to study a wide range of decentralized systems, including blockchain, consensus protocols, and decentralized machine learning algorithms.  In this research, the design and implementation of Kollaps are presented, along with a case study demonstrating its application in emulating the behavior of a consensus network.

We delve into the geometric underpinnings of the Newman-Penrose map, 
which transforms 3D asymptotically flat space-time metrics to conformally 
flat 3D spaces with constant curvature - either positive, negative or flat. 
This map is defined by the relationship between the twistor space of the 
initial metric and its compactified version, which is achievable through 
projective completion in the complex projective 3-space CP^3. The resulting 
conformal structure in 3-space is derived from the curvature tensor of the 
twistor space, specifically the Weyl tensor, thereby establishing a deeper 
connection between the initial and resulting geometries. This theoretical 
understanding offers a new perspective on the twistor theory and the 
Newman-Penrose map, and also sheds light on the behavior of asymptotically flat 
spaces in relation to the behavior of their twistor space.

The Muon Tomography project aims to create detailed maps of underground structures using muons as a tracing agent. This involves sending muons through the earth and analyzing the changes in the muon flux to build a 3D image of the underground environment. The goal is to utilize this technique for detecting and mapping nuclear waste in existing facilities around the world. This paper details the development of a muon detector capable of capturing data in the field, including data acquisition and analysis software. The detector consists of two layers of silicon photodetectors, each with a large total area of about 7 square meters, detecting muons traveling in two distinct directions. The detector is made up of 64 individual photodetectors, providing a high degree of spatial resolution. The system is powered by an advanced readout system, which enables precise measurement of both the timing and spatial coordinates of the detected muons. The detector's angular resolution is approximately 3.9 degrees, providing a comprehensive view of the surrounding area. The Muon Tomography project has successfully demonstrated its detector in a controlled environment, and the results are presented in this paper.

This study introduces a new LLP parsing expression grammar implementation, providing a detailed explanation of the parsing process and demonstrating its efficiency in handling complex scenarios, specifically through the resolution of a practical practical example: parsing a zip archive and then extracting a file within it.

In this research, we investigate the properties of a classical abelian Proca theory under the influence of temperature. Using the Schwinger proper time technique, we demonstrate that thermal effects introduce a temperature-dependent mass squared term into the vacuum propagation, effectively creating a new inertial mass. When the Schwinger proper time approaches its maximum value, the mass term becomes negligible, much like in the zero-temperature scenario, although at finite temperatures it remains non-zero. Furthermore, our analysis shows that this temperature-dependent mass leads to a new, temperature-adjusted radiation condition. When the Compton wavelength is much larger than the distance between source and detector, the radiation condition aligns with the classical one, whereas if the Compton wavelength is smaller than this distance, the radiation condition diverges from its classical counterpart. These findings can be applied to various areas of research, including the study of Proca theory in the presence of thermal fluctuations, the quantum electrodynamics of strong fields, and the physics of relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

To study how language changes over time, researchers have been tracking the development
of English using a unique dataset of books written over the last 500 years. This approach
involves using pre-trained deep neural networks to make predictions about future language
patterns, and a novel technique to analyze these forecasts and compare it with historical data.
This method provides a clear path to a quantitative understanding of how language evolves
and can be applied to other areas beyond linguistics such as modeling human behavior.

We propose an approach to determine the three-dimensional pose of an object
solely by observing its movement when it is turned. This method, referred to as
'Debug Rotation', leverages the fact that when an object rotates, its movement
can be attributed to both its rotation and a fixed, internal axis. By utilizing
an unsupervised learning algorithm, this approach can identify an object's
orientation without prior knowledge of its shape, shape characteristics or
position in space. The effectiveness of 'Debug Rotation' is demonstrated by
applying it to both the Carrot19 dataset and a large, publicly available dataset
of real-world vehicles, achieving a 7.9% reduction in the error of three-
dimensional pose estimation for the former dataset and real-world performance
comparable to other leading methods.

In this investigation, we demonstrate the manipulation of Andreev bound states through an applied magnetic field, which significantly influences the controlled crossover between the dominant phenomena of elastic reflection and crossed Andreev reflection. A novel device design featuring an SNS Josephson junction with an integrated quantum dot allows for the precise tuning of the magnetic field to switch between the two dominant effects. Furthermore, our research reveals that the magnitude of both effects is proportional to the square of the amplitude of the dominant Andreev bound state, which can be precisely controlled via the magnetic field. Utilizing a simple tight-binding model, our numerical analysis based on the Green function formalism confirms the feasibility of achieving a substantial ratio of crossed Andreev reflection to coherent perfect elastic reflection. Our findings have the potential to be experimentally verified in systems such as carbon nanotubes, graphene nanotubes, or semiconductor quantum dots.

A novel approach to three-dimensional kinetic simulations of magnetic reconnection
involves incorporating ad hoc angle-scattering to model the interaction between
gyrocentris and bulk motions. This method is applied to a test case of
perpendicular half-steady-state reconnection. It is found that the simulated
results can replicate the nonthermal particle acceleration in the form of a
power-law distribution that is in line with previous research, especially when
major ion anisotropy is present. This simulated framework offers a more
realistic description of kinetic physics, especially in scenarios where the
gyrocenter motion is dominant.

We investigate the impact of extended scalar sectors on the $e^+e^- \to Zh$ and $\gamma\gamma \to H$ processes, particularly focusing on the most feasible scenarios. In the case of $e^+e^- \to Zh$, we consider two main types of models: one with a singlet scalar and the other with a doublet scalar. The singlet scalar model is associated with a light Higgs boson, while the doublet scalar model is linked to the 125 GeV Higgs. We also examine the impact of extended scalar sectors on the diphoton decays of the Higgs boson, taking into account the minimal extension of the SM Higgs sector. Our analysis reveals that future experiments on $e^+e^- \to Zh$ and $\gamma\gamma \to H$ can significantly constrain the parameter space of the singlet scalar model and the doublet scalar model, respectively.

This paper presents an alternative definition of the subdifferential for the combined numerical radius, further developing upon the work of L. Lee and P. Netzer. As a result, it is possible to derive additional inequalities for the combined numerical radius, which are estimated and proven based on this alternative definition.

The concept of differential privacy has gained significant attention in recent years, primarily due to its ability to ensure data privacy's reliability. In this paper, we focus on financial differential privacy applications, aiming to enhance the financial sector's security. We have identified two primary contributions. Firstly, we introduce novel financial applications of differential privacy across multiple areas, including financial services, financial data, and financial security. Secondly, we outline the differential privacy requirements and challenges inherent to the financial sector, proposing potential solutions.

This paper explores a novel method for describing dependent vector-valued stochastic processes using stochastic transformations and random dispersion fields. The study focuses on stochastic mappings that preserve the absolute or relative continuity of their initial distributions, establishing that these mappings can be represented by a function related to a normal order. The primary contribution of this paper is in the field of dependent statistics, where it derives conditions for the existence of a stochastic mapping between two distributions in both one and multi-dimensional settings. The study also examines the properties of dependent random dispersion fields, which are defined as field functions associated with normal orders. The results establish that a random dispersion field exists if its conditional dispersion does not depend on the choice of normal order.

Research has shown that high-energy, nanosecond and sub-nanosecond lasers can be used to ignite high-pressure, inert gas-buried combustible gas mixtures. This study investigates the ignition of He, He+H2+O2 mixtures under the conditions of 1.5-3.5 times standard pressure, with He, O2, and H2 ratios of 95:5:0.5 and 50:50:1 respectively. The ignition was achieved by using a 3D, uncollimated laser beam with a 1.5 nanosecond pulse duration. The study found that the ignition energy of He, He+H2+O2 mixtures was 0.1 J and 0.5 J respectively. The study found that the He gas suppressed the combustion of H2+O2 mixtures. The study found that the He gas also suppressed the combustion of H2+O2+air mixtures at a pressure of 1.5 bar. The study found that the He gas also suppressed the combustion of H2+O2+air mixtures at a pressure of 3.5 bar.

Deep learning techniques have revolutionized semantic segmentation, with the development of fully convolutional networks capable of producing pixel-level predictions. However, these models struggle with accurately delineating object boundaries due to their reliance on convolution operations. This limitation is further exacerbated by data augmentation techniques that often distort object boundaries during image processing. To address this challenge, we introduce a new boundary-focused module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures to enhance their boundary detection capabilities. This module is designed to be highly parameter and computation efficient, making it suitable for integration into various network architectures, including mobile and web applications. Furthermore, we introduce a new boundary-based loss function that can be used in conjunction with existing loss functions to improve overall network performance. This function is particularly effective in refining the network's boundary delineation and can be used in conjunction with other loss functions to achieve better results. We evaluate the performance of our approach on the CamVid and Cityscapes datasets, with the mobile application achieving a significant improvement in mean IoU score from 60.0 to 65.8, while the web application saw an even more substantial improvement from 59.0 to 72.1.

This research proposes a driver messenger system, enabling communication between drivers by broadcasting essential vehicle information. The system, consisting of two components - a local processing unit and a central server - facilitates the exchange of vehicle data among nearby vehicles. The local system, powered by an ARM Cortex-M0 microcontroller, optimizes energy consumption and processing speed. The system's effectiveness is showcased through a lane change assistance application, which demonstrates the benefits of intervehicle information sharing. Additionally, the system's performance is evaluated using real-world data and a cost-benefit analysis to determine its feasibility in next-generation vehicle networks.

The movement of non-interacting, weakly active particles in space is influenced by the presence or absence of boundaries. In this research, we examine how different types of boundaries affect the particles' steady-state distribution and the direction of their mean flow. Using the active Brownian motion model, we derive exact solutions for various geometries with either absorbing or reflecting boundaries, and then use these results to derive approximate solutions for more complex scenarios. Our findings reveal that boundaries significantly impact both the direction and magnitude of the mean flow, and also shape the distribution of particle positions, with certain boundaries causing particles to accumulate near these points. Furthermore, our results show that boundaries can also affect the particles' speed, causing them to slow down when encountering an absorbing boundary or speed up when encountering a reflecting boundary.

The Average Particle Model, a shell model based on random two-body interactions, is used to study the excitation of nuclei with square-integral interactions. This model is capable of generating a wide range of interaction strengths, from weak to strong coupling, allowing for a detailed analysis of nuclear behavior. In this study, we focus on the effects of Siegert states within the model, which are states resulting from breaking the pair symmetry. We find that Siegert states significantly influence the distribution of energy between single-particle and collective modes, particularly at high-energy levels. In fact, the energy dissipation of Siegert states is found to be comparable to that of quadrupole collective modes, indicating a substantial impact on the nuclear deformation. This discovery suggests that Siegert states should be considered when developing effective nuclear interactions for low-lying structure calculations.

Observations of the Si IV 1390-6 A doublet from an X1.1 solar flare reveal significant changes in its properties, such as intensity, line width, and spectral shape during flare peak. Notably, line width and intensity exhibit a direct correlation with each other, and both show a notable increase of about 50% during flare peak. High-resolution spectra of this flare were obtained using the French-Primeau solar abundance model, and 3D MHD simulations by Schrijver et al. (2011) suggest that the enhanced intensity is primarily due to coronal heating. However, the correlation between line width and intensity is thought to be the result of non-thermal effects, and this is supported by the French-Primeau solar abundance model, and 3D MHD simulations by Schrijner et al. (2011) reveal that the spectral broadening is caused by a mixture of ions with different charge states.

The strong CP problem remains unsolved, and its existence implies the presence of a hypothetical particle known as the axion. However, recent studies indicate that this particle may not be light, which would resolve the strong CP issue but create a significant electric dipole moment for neutrons. Measuring this moment accurately will provide insight into the axion mass, potentially revealing whether it exists within a range that resolves the strong CP problem. If the axion mass exceeds $10^{-5}$ eV, it will not be sufficient to resolve the strong CP problem.

A detailed examination of the impact of the spatial distribution of energy deposited by an ion beam on the optical properties of thin films reveals that it significantly affects the critical angle associated with self-organization. By comparing simulations of the energy distribution with experimental measurements, the spatial distribution of the energy deposited by the ion beam on the thin film is determined. This allows the investigation of the relationship between the spatial distribution of the energy and the underlying causes of the thin film's self-organization. A detailed analysis of the movement and energy loss of atoms within the thin film due to the ion beam leads to the identification of the physical mechanisms responsible for the self-organization.

In software engineering, accurately identifying plagiarism is a pressing concern, yet existing detection methods primarily focus on identifying stolen intellectual property from sources like articles and books. Our contribution presents an innovative, automated tool called antiPlag that leverages the white-box AntiPLAG approach to detect plagiarism within individual software sources. By employing the Structural Pathway method, antiPlag can pinpoint structural plagiarism in a software system. A novel two-stage process was developed to detect and eliminate structural plagiarism, and antiPlag is capable of detecting various forms of plagiarism, including structural and textual. Additionally, we have adapted the AntiPLAG approach to accommodate C# programming standards and incorporated it into antiPlag. Experimental results demonstrate that antiPlag excels in detecting structural plagiarism within C# software sources.

The article explores the full convergence of certain automorphic Dirichlet series. Initially, the framework is established in the context of $\mathrm{GL}(n)$ over the rational numbers. Next, the discussion is redirected to a general reductive group F over a finite set of valued fields. An extension of the Poincaré-Legendre theorem is achieved, confirming the full convergence of automorphic Dirichlet series related to Fourier-Jacobi coefficients for the given group F under specific conditions. An analogous outcome is also obtained for a specific class of automorphic Dirichlet series associated with Siegel-Jugate functionals.

This letter demonstrates that every complete metric space X with the property that distance is uniformly restricted at every point, can be divided into subsets where the metric behavior is uniform across all points within each subset.

We introduce Concave, a fast and efficient tool for estimating densities that follow a log-concave pattern. Our approach utilizes Matheron's method, a sampling technique combined with Newton's method, to determine the density parameters. Concave is highly versatile and can handle a wide range of log-concave densities, including those defined on higher-dimensional spaces. The tool is easily installed via a single command and produces reliable results. Concave is available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/jesr52/Concave. The associated R code for the study can be found at https://github.com/jesr52/Concave-Research.

To efficiently explore numerous stable states in granular systems, researchers have developed a novel Monte Carlo sampling approach, which utilizes an energy arch-based microstate network. This method, which focuses on the volume-based ensemble, allows for the identification of stable states and facilitates the calculation of associated entropy values. By implementing this approach, the entropy of various granular systems can be determined, with the entropy scale serving as a measure of packing diversity. This method, which can be applied to a wide range of granular systems, offers valuable insights into their structural properties.

We investigate a game for Graphs, referred to as the Adventurer-Director game, in which two players are involved. The Adventurer moves from vertex to vertex of a given graph while adhering to the Director's instructions, aiming to execute an action at a pre-designated target vertex with the Adventurer's initial placement also considered significant. Our research focuses on determining optimal Adventurer and Director winning strategies, as well as the minimum number of required Adventurer moves and a detailed description of an optimal Director strategy for winning scenarios. Our study demonstrates that Adventurer can guarantee no more than one additional Graph step compared to the shortest Adventurer path to the target, and further analysis provides upper and lower bounds on the maximum value of an optimally directed action, and identifies specific cases where Adventurer can accomplish this action in a minimal number of steps or no more than one additional step from the shortest Adventurer path to the target, and provides a precise description of an optimal Adventurer strategy for winning scenarios.

The fluctuation theorems provide a general understanding of probability distributions of thermodynamic variables under nonequilibrium conditions. Building on this principle, the probability distribution of the Fourier components of thermodynamic variables for Gaussian processes has been derived. This analysis enables the calculation of the joint probability distribution of Fourier components at various frequencies. Notably, frequency-dependent relationships emerge in the probability distribution and correlations between Fourier components become evident. This research offers insights into understanding correlations among Fourier components and validates the findings with numerical simulations of the nonequilibrium work distribution on an example system.

This study focuses on the one-dimensional, higher-order Broer-Kaup system. We use the method of differential elimination to convert the system into a pair of coupled nonlinear partial differential equations, and then use the soliton-like solution method to analyze the behavior of the resulting solutions. Additionally, two potential interaction scenarios involving solitons in the solution are examined.

We establish the existence of weak solutions to the incompressible Euler equations that conserve energy. These solutions are characterized by having finite energy at all points in space. Our approach builds on the work of others, specifically the works of Di Nezza-Ponzo-Spasciano and Gamburtseva-Li-Yang. Our proof primarily focuses on demonstrating the integrability of the vorticity.

The Virtual Reality Project, VIRUP, is a cutting-edge innovation that generates immersive virtual environments for the benefit of people with neurological disorders. Its innovative features include customized environments that enhance cognitive functions and positively influence emotional states. The project's website, located at http://www.virtualrealityproject.org, showcases its latest advancements and serves as a resource for public awareness. Recent updates to the project's website have been supported by the International Disabled Association organization.

This paper presents "Space Voyage," an educational board game designed to teach
kids the basic principles of data and its management. The game aims to make
learning data software engineering engaging and approachable for the next
generation of data scientists. The developed board game is a result of our
participation in 2022's Data Science Education Awards.

In software-defined networking (SDN), the switch operates solely based on the instructions provided by the SDN controller, which is usually a logical representation of the entire network. This leads to a unique characteristic where the switch only processes a limited set of data flows at any given time, which we call "operational data-flows." Focusing on these data-flows can offer a clearer view of the actual network behavior. This paper proposes a method to identify these data-flows in real-time using a combination of switch and controller analysis. Our approach is based on the concept that data-flows are present in the controller if and only if they are operational in the switch. We have tested this approach on various network scenarios and found that it can accurately identify data-flows with a high degree of precision.

Recent advancements in VAEs have led to the development of models capable of learning weakly disentangled representations, which have been shown to effectively capture the object's identity and pose. However, these representations often fail to account for the object's pose when the object is viewed from a different angle. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method that leverages relational information between different views, which enables the model to learn a more comprehensive set of weakly disentangled features. By utilizing this approach, our model can learn a variety of representations, including object identity, pose, and view. Through our experiments on the 3D shape and pose dataset, we have found that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models by learning more effective representations of pose and view.

In the realm of ocean energy harvesting using oscillating foils, the wake foil concept has garnered significant attention, where the trailing foil synchronizes its movement with the leading foil to optimize energy gains. A study was conducted to examine the effect of this synchronization on an oscillating foil of varying lengths, focusing on the interplay between the two foils and its impact on energy efficiency. The investigation revealed that when the two foils are out of sync, the shorter trailing foil surpasses the longer one in terms of energy collection. Conversely, when synchronized, the longer foil outperforms the shorter one under specific conditions. Notably, the synchronization of the two foils does not significantly alter the dynamic wake pattern, but rather enhances the previously established efficiency improvements through the length of the trailing foil.

We've developed a Bayesian method to study the real-time dynamics of lattice QCD by simulating various thermal states. This method involves analyzing thermal correlation functions while factoring in systematic and statistical uncertainties to obtain more reliable results. Unlike traditional methods, our approach enables precise control over the accuracy of the results, allowing us to derive precise error bars for real-time quantities. Additionally, we can validate the accuracy of the results by cross-checking them against the underlying lattice data, ensuring that the uncertainty margins are correctly calibrated. This method can be applied to a wide range of problems, including the thermal evolution of quark-gluon plasma and the scattering of gluons in complex systems.

In this work, we investigate the charge-tunneling phenomenon between a quantum dot and a superconducting island, using advanced gate sensing to gather information on the quantum dot's charge state. By utilizing a quantum point contact as a highly sensitive and fast-gating gate, we can accurately determine when the quantum dot enters a supercurrent state, enabling us to reconstruct the entire charge tunneling spectrum. Our findings indicate that when the Coulomb interaction is present, the supercurrent state is achieved through a process where the quantum dot is occupied by an odd number of electrons, resulting in an Andreev bound state. Conversely, in the absence of Coulomb interaction, the supercurrent state is facilitated by a process known as Majorana bound state formation. Our research provides the first charge tunneling spectrum obtained through the employment of a quantum point contact as a sensing gate, thereby opening up new avenues for studying quantum systems.

Developing effective new medicines is a slow and expensive process, often taking more than a decade to complete. To speed up this process, researchers have been using artificial intelligence to generate new candidate compounds that have good properties but, so far, have struggled to find candidates that work well as treatments. To address this issue, our research introduces a new model called Energy-driven Generative Models (EdGMs). EdGMs are specifically designed to generate new compounds that have the desired properties and are suitable for treating a particular disease. We tested EdGMs on a common genetic disorder, sickle cell anemia, and found that the generated compounds are more likely to be effective than those found using previous methods. EdGMs use a unique combination of information, including the structure of molecules and their interactions with other substances, to evaluate how well a compound would work as a treatment. We found that the generated compounds in our study had higher effectiveness scores and more potential as treatments compared to those produced by other models.

The Graph Structure of Interaction (GSI) language offers an efficient way
to create graph-based programming languages where the graph serves as the
basis for both execution and development. GGI is a modified version of GSI,
introduced by the author, which relies on a data structure called token to
guide the graph-based program. GGI stands out as an efficient way for
developing two-sided graphs where the token acts as the central control unit.
By integrating dynamic geometry of interaction, GGI enables developers to
create interactive systems where the program and interactions are deeply
integrated.

The Large Magellanic Cloud's (LMC) structure and evolution are influenced by its interaction with the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). By examining the motion of LMC stars, astronomers can gain insight into the impact of this interaction. Using proper motion and photometric data from the Vienna Survey of the Magellanic Clouds, astronomers analyzed the motion of stars in the outer LMC, beyond the supernova 2017aaa explosion site, and compared it to similar data from the SMC. The results revealed that stars in the outer LMC exhibit consistent motion patterns, with a significant 30 km/s velocity difference in the direction of the SMC, and minimal motion perpendicular to the LMC-SMC plane. The observed differences in proper motion between the LMC and SMC suggest that the SMC's gravitational pull is causing the motion of the LMC's outer stars, with the SMC's distance from the LMC resulting in a significant 30 km/s velocity difference and corresponding tidal forces.

Deep learning models require a substantial amount of parameters, and determining their optimal settings is a complex process, often necessitating extensive expertise and additional time for hyper-parameter fine-tuning. This process can be particularly daunting when working with limited data. This paper presents a novel approach to automatically select the best hyper-parameters for recurrent neural networks in a manner that minimizes computational costs. By utilizing an evolutionary algorithm, this approach is able to efficiently select the optimal hyper-settings, thereby enhancing the detection capabilities of these models for identifying power theft in smart grid systems. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance in real-world scenarios, surpassing even expert-tuned models and yielding significant improvements in terms of accuracy, precision, and recall.
Compact surfaces equipped with a boundary can be decomposed into alternating regions of convex and concave character when their edge-based graphs are divided in a specific inducive manner.

Using a 1.0/fb dataset from proton-proton collisions at the LHCb detector, 
the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons are produced in $p p \to p \Omega^{0}_{c} \pi^-$ and $p p \to p \Xi^{0}_{c} \pi^-$ channels, 
and their lifetimes are measured via the decay $ {\Omega^{0}_{c}} \to \Xi^{-} K^{+} \pi^{+} \pi^{-} $ and $ {\Xi^{0}_{c}} \to \Xi^{-} K^{+} \pi^{+} \pi^{-} $.
The results show the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ lifetime is $ 280.1 \pm 2.4 \pm 2.1 \pm 1.7 $ ps and the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ lifetime is $ 1.400 \pm 0.005 \pm 0.009 \pm 0.010 $ ps.
The errors are attributed to statistical analysis, detector calibration, and the uncertainty of the production cross-sections, 
respectively. These results are consistent with current established values and will help refine the determination of the $SU(3)$ mass differences between heavy-flavour baryons.

Hyperspectral image classification is a critical task in remote sensing with various applications. It's a complex problem due to the high dimensionality of HSI data, which hinders classification accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework for subspace-based HSI classification, aiming to enhance efficiency and precision. Initially, we propose an innovative spectral-spatial-spatial feature extraction method that combines local sparse representation with spatial-spatial auto-encoder learning. This method decomposes HSI data into spatial-spatial features and spatial spectral features. A spatial-spatial auto-encoder is then trained to extract spatial-spatial features from the original data, while a local sparse auto-encoder extracts spatial spectral features. Finally, we utilize the spatial-spatial and spatial spectral features to obtain final class labels through a discriminative classifier. Experimental results on three HSI datasets demonstrate the proposed approach's efficacy and efficiency.

Arctic sea ice's surface features small-scale undulations, formed by the accumulation of snow that alters local wind and temperature patterns, and in turn affects the snow ridge itself.  Despite the importance of these features, current sea-ice models struggle to accurately replicate their Arctic presence while being too sensitive to subgrid-scale snow accumulation.  A more realistic representation is needed to understand how changing Arctic ice cover impacts sea ice stability.  A new approach to modeling Arctic ice cover has been developed which incorporates the key factors driving snow-ice interaction, and initial results show it successfully replicates the presence of these features in the Arctic.  By isolating the specific processes that lead to snow ridge formation, this model offers a valuable tool to investigate how changing Arctic ice cover impacts sea ice stability, and can be used to inform the development of more advanced sea-ice models in the future.

We investigate the quantum Zeno effect of ultracold atom-molecule scattering in oscillating magnetic fields, revealing that rapid measurements significantly suppress the final state population by eliminating the time-dependent oscillations between the initial and final states. Notably, the scattering probability is greatly diminished when the oscillation frequency matches the transition frequency between the initial and final states. This phenomenon allows for the development of a precise technique for detecting scattering by rapidly measuring outcomes, as well as distinguishing between transitions and preventing them by carefully designing the oscillation frequency. The application of this method to ultracold mixtures of bosonic Rb atoms and molecules provides promising avenues for studying and controlling such systems.

This research introduces a novel It\^o-Langevin dynamics model that deviates from classical mechanics through its non-conservative, non-thermalizable behavior governed by a q-Gaussian distribution. A novel stochastic process is presented, which is non-thermalizable and exhibits a q-Gaussian distribution, characterized by a Q parameter. A new It\^i-Langevin model is introduced, which is non-thermalizable and characterized by a q-Poisson distribution under specific conditions. These dynamics are naturally generated by a q-Markovian process. A novel, non-thermalizable Gibbs-Boltzmann equation is derived, which incorporates a q-exponential distribution under specific conditions. These dynamics are naturally generated by a q-Markovian process. These stochastic processes and dynamics are naturally interconnected via a q-deformed Gibbs-Boltzmann Gibbs-Bose equation. These non-thermalizable stochastic processes and dynamics are naturally interconnected via a q-deformed Gibbs-Boltzmann Gibbs-Bose equation. It is hypothesized that these non-thermalizable dynamics can be naturally explained by a q-Markovian process. These non-thermalizable dynamics can be naturally explained by a q-Markovian process.

A novel class of topological semimetals, characterized by nodal lines, has garnered significant attention. The breaking of spatial or temporal symmetries in these materials leads to unique topological features, such as Weyl points. In this study, we demonstrate the creation of a higher-order topological semimetal using optical techniques. The results reveal that when a nodal semimetal is exposed to two laser beams with a frequency matching its band gap, it undergoes a transition into a higher-order Weyl semimetal. The work showcases the potential of optical control in manipulating topological phases.

The increasing global demand for cloud computing has led to a growing need for secure, decentralized, and efficient solutions. To address this need, we propose the decentralized and blockchain-based computing protocol, Marvel DC, which can coexist with most existing systems. Marvel DC utilizes a unique consensus model to ensure the reliability of user tasks and computing power, offering a scalable solution that can handle varying computing requirements. Marvel DC seamlessly integrates a wide range of computational resources, outpacing its competitors in performance while ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of user data. In a real-world test, our system successfully completed 85% of tasks from stardust, a popular machine learning library. With its advanced security features and high throughput, Marvel DC is poised to revolutionize cloud computing by providing users with a secure, decentralized, and intelligent platform.

This paper introduces a reduced reference perceptual quality assessment framework tailored to 3D point cloud compression, which is a critical evaluation metric. The proposed framework incorporates a comprehensive quality assessment model, a reference encoding method, and a set of distortion metrics. The RR-QA framework facilitates the development of an optimized rate control mechanism for 3D point cloud lossless compression, which is meticulously examined and validated through extensive testing.

In holographic QCD, the strong coupling regime of QCD can be replicated.
By adjusting the 't Hooft parameter, the holographic QCD phase diagram can be mapped.
We've established that the deconfinement transition can be modeled as a thermal transition when the 't Hooft parameter is large.
We've also discovered that at lower 't Hooft parameters, the deconfinement transition and chiral transition can occur separately.
Consequently, the QCD phase diagram can be reconstructed using holography, and we've found that the critical points for the deconfinement and chiral transitions align.
This alignment is consistent across different gauge conditions and lattice spacings.

Knee joint osteoarthritis is a widespread orthopedic condition that affects millions of people globally. To diagnose this condition, doctors frequently utilize MRI scans in combination with clinical data. However, MRI-based diagnosis is a costly and time-consuming process. To address this issue, researchers have developed a novel framework that utilizes 3D MRI data to identify early-stage knee joint osteoarthritis. This framework leverages a combination of self-supervised learning and data slicing to analyze the knee joint's cartilage and synovial tissue. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in classification accuracy, achieving a 3.5% improvement on the OA-3D dataset. Additionally, the use of data slicing has been demonstrated to enhance the effectiveness of the model's output.

This study presents a few-shot typeface generation (FSTG) method, aiming to create new typefaces quickly from limited samples. The generation challenge arises from the difficulty of accurately capturing the distinctive styles of each font, which are often lost in the process of generalizing to a wide range of fonts. To address this problem, we propose a new approach that learns to recognize and replicate the unique, distinctive styles present within each font, rather than relying on a general understanding of fonts. By leveraging a new attention-based method, our approach can learn from a single example to generate new typefaces that closely resemble the original font, achieving this even when only one or two examples are available.
